O mankind,[1] be Mindful[2] of your Lord.[3] Indeed, the Convulsion[4] of the Hour is a tremendous thing.

[1] The sura contains four all-inclusive calls to mankind, in Ayas 1, 5, 49 and 73. Although the address “O mankind” is universal in wording, its immediate historical horizon most pointedly confronts the Deniers of Makkah, who rejected the Message, denied resurrection and the coming of the Final Hour, Associated false deities with their Lord and Nurturer, and relentlessly opposed the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Believers. Thus, while the call embraces all humanity, its sharpest edge in this context is directed towards those who stood in active opposition to the Truth. In these four addresses, God Almighty variously warns of the terror of the Hour, calls people to reflect upon the Signs of creation as proof of resurrection, declares the Messenger’s role as a clear warner, and exposes the utter impotence of false deities through the parable of the fly. Ibn ʿĀshīūr observes that the people who fall first under the address “O mankind” are the Makkan Associators, though its wording remains general. Among the subtle eloquences of the Qur’an is that the opening, “O mankind, be Mindful of your Lord”, introduces two suras. The first is Sīūrat al-Nisāʾ, the fourth sura of what al-Rāzī calls the first half of the Qur’an, where Mindfulness is grounded in knowledge of the Origin: God created mankind from a single soul, manifesting the perfection of His Power, Knowledge and Wisdom. The second is Sīūrat al-Ḥajj, which al-Rāzī likewise calls the fourth sura of the second half, counting Maryam, Ṭā Hā, al-Anbiyāʾ and then al-Ḥajj. Here Mindfulness is grounded in knowledge of the Return through the terrifying Convulsion of the Hour. The two openings therefore point respectively to the Origin and the Return, with creation preceding resurrection, a subtle correspondence in the Divinely ordained ordering of the suras (cf. al-Rāzī, Abīū Ḥayyān, Ibn ʿĀdil).
 [2] Be Mindful of your Lord, the One Who created you, Who provides for you and governs your affairs, by complying with His commands and shunning His prohibitions (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī).
 [3] Expressing the Divine Essence by the title Rabb (Lord, Nurturer), and annexing it to the addressees (“your Rabb”), subtly signals both His worthiness to be feared by virtue of His Majestic Creatorship and sustaining governance, and mankind’s obligation to be Mindful of Him, since His commands and prohibitions are solely for their welfare and protection from harm. This nuance is conveyed more fully by Rabb than by titles such as Creator or Master. (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [4] Zalzalah denotes violent shaking or severe convulsion. The word is related to zalla ʿan al-mawḍiʿ, to slip or move from one’s place, suggesting repeated displacement and movement (cf. al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb). Exegetes discuss two related questions concerning “the Convulsion of the Hour”: its nature and its timing. Regarding its nature, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reports that the majority understand it as a real convulsion resembling earthquakes known in this worldly life, but of incomparably greater severity. Ibn ʿĀshīūr likewise considers the literal meaning the more apparent, while allowing that zalzalah may also be used figuratively for the overwhelming terrors of the Hour. Ibn Juzayy similarly records both possibilities: the severity and horrors of the Hour, or the actual shaking of the Earth (cf. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn Juzayy, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). Regarding its timing, many exegetes place it at the end of this worldly life, before resurrection. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, al-Qurṭubī and Abīū Ḥayyān report this as the majority view, and Ibn Juzayy and Ibn ʿĀshīūr prefer it. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah also notes that the mention of nursing mothers and pregnant women lends support to this interpretation (cf. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, al-Qurṭubī, Abīū Ḥayyān, Ibn Juzayy, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). al-Ṭabarī and al-Shinqīṭī, however, prefer the view that it occurs after people have been raised from their graves, basing this on authentic reports in which the Prophet (ﷺ) connects these ayas with God’s command to Adam to bring forth the contingent destined for the Fire. al-Shinqīṭī considers this evidence decisive. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah responds that the hadith need not determine the precise timing of the Convulsion: the Prophet (ﷺ) may have recited ayas describing the beginning of the Hour and then proceeded to describe a later scene of the Day of Judgement. It follows that the authentic report explains the close connection between the ayas and that terrible scene without necessarily ending the exegetical disagreement over when the Convulsion itself takes place. Abīū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (رضي الله عنه) narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: “Allah says, ‘O Adam!’ He replies, ‘At Your service and pleasure; all good is in Your Hands.’ He says, ‘Bring forth the contingent of the Fire.’ He asks, ‘What is the contingent of the Fire?’ He says, ‘From every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine.’ At that moment, the young will turn grey, every pregnant one will lay down her burden, and you will see mankind as though intoxicated, though they are not intoxicated; but Allah’s Punishment is severe...” The Prophet (ﷺ) then reassured his Companions that the overwhelming number would be from Gog and Magog, and expressed his hope that his community would constitute half the people of Paradise (al-Bukhārī: 3348; Muslim: 222).

On the Day you behold it; every nursing mother shall be stupefied[1] [and forget] what she is suckling, and every female possessed of a pregnancy shall cast down her burden;[2] and you [onlooker] shall see people [as though] intoxicated,[3] yet they are not intoxicated—rather, the Punishment of Allah is severe.[4]

[1] Tadhhalu: that is, she forgets and neglects. Dhuhīūl denotes being distracted from something that, under ordinary circumstances, one would have every reason to remember. The root dh-h-l conveys absence of mind or distraction caused by terror or some overwhelming preoccupation (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān). That is, when mankind behold the Convulsion of the Hour, every nursing mother will be so overwhelmed by its terror that she will become distracted even from the child she is nursing, despite the powerful natural bond and immediate concern that ordinarily hold her attention (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr).
 [2] Every pregnant female will deliver what she carries before its term, overcome by the terror and anguish of that Day (cf. Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī). The expression dhātu ḥaml [literally, “one possessed of a pregnancy”, or “one carrying a burden”] is more expressive than simply ḥāmil [“pregnant”]. Whereas ḥāmil merely describes the state of being pregnant, dhātu ḥaml draws attention to what is being carried and to its intimate attachment to the one carrying it. The wording thereupon heightens the horror of the scene: even that which is most closely and naturally bound to its bearer is prematurely cast off under the overwhelming terror of the Hour (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [3] The onlooker takes them to be intoxicated, their minds confounded and their awareness eclipsed by overwhelming terror; yet, they are not truly intoxicated. Their condition merely resembles drunkenness because of the severity of what they witness (cf. al-Samarqandī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī).
 [4] The Hour bursts forth with overwhelming force, shattering every illusion of permanence and security. The scene is one of all-encompassing convulsion, whether understood as the violent shaking of the Earth itself or as encompassing the overwhelming terror that seizes those who witness it. Composure dissolves and even the strongest natural attachments are momentarily eclipsed. A mother in the very act of nursing, absorbed in the care of the child at her breast, becomes so overwhelmed that she is distracted from the one she nurses. Every pregnant one delivers what she carries before its term. What under ordinary circumstances commands the most immediate care and attention is forgotten under the terror of the Hour. Humanity staggers beneath its impact. Minds are confounded and awareness overwhelmed; people appear intoxicated, disoriented, and unsteady, though they are not truly intoxicated. Their condition resembles drunkenness only because of the severity of the terror confronting them. The spectacle reaches both outward experience and inward consciousness: whatever the precise nature of the zalzalah, its effect upon those who behold the Hour is one of utter bewilderment, in which ordinary composure and awareness give way before the enormity of what unfolds.
[1]Among people is one who disputes concerning Allah without knowledge,[2] and follows every mutinous devil,[3]

[1] This clause contrasts the universal call to Mindfulness with the response of those who turn away from it, disputing concerning God without knowledge. Their dispute concerns His Oneness, Attributes and Message, and is characterised not by sincere inquiry but by fallacious argument, sophistry, eloquence and deceptive presentation. Ibn ʿĀshīūr identifies such disputants particularly with the leaders of Association, whose influence misleads others and obstructs them from following the Truth. He observes that the particular mention of these leaders suggests that, were it not for their misleading influence and obstruction, many among the Associators would incline towards Islam because of the manifest strength of its proof and its accord with sound human nature. “Following every rebellious devil” means yielding uncritically to satanic whisperings without subjecting them to reflection or sound reasoning. Although al-Naḍr Ibn al-Ḥārith is mentioned as a specific immediate referent, the wording remains general and encompasses everyone who disputes concerning God without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr). al-Ṭabarī also transmits the report concerning al-Naḍr Ibn al-Ḥārith, who disputed God’s Power to resurrect the dead.
 [2] They dispute concerning God Almighty and His religion without knowledge, arguing from corrupt judgement and distorted reasoning and seeking in that way to uphold falsehood and invalidate Truth. Their dispute includes denying God’s Oneness and His Power to resurrect the dead, and rejecting the truth brought by His Messengers (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Nasafī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). al-Nasafī records both a specific interpretation referring to al-Naḍr Ibn al-Ḥārith and a general one encompassing anyone who disputes about religion according to caprice. al-Ṭabarī particularly relates the dispute to denial of God’s Power to resurrect the dead, while Ibn Kathīr extends it to rejection of the revealed Truth.
 [3] In their ignorant disputation concerning God, they follow every deeply rebellious devil from among mankind and jinn. Marīd denotes one hardened in rebellion and evil, devoid of goodness. They readily yield to such satanic whisperings and act upon them without hesitation or subjecting them to reflection and sound proof (cf. al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
upon whom it is written that whoever takes him (such a devil) as an ally, that he will surely mislead him to the Punishment of the Blaze.

[1]O people, if you are in [sceptical] misgiving[2] concerning the Resurrection, then indeed We have created you from dust,[3] then from a drop,[4] then from a clinging clot,[5] then from a morsel of flesh,[6] formed and unformed,[7] so that We may make [this][8] clear to you.[9] And We cause to settle in the wombs what We Will until an appointed term;[10] then We bring you forth [each] as an infant;[11] then so that you may reach your full strength.[12] And among you is he who is taken in death, and among you is he who is returned to the lowest stage of life,[13] so that he may know nothing after having possessed [some] knowledge.[14] [15]And you see the land barren and lifeless;[16] then when We send down water upon it,[17] it stirs,[18] swells,[19] and brings forth of every delightful kind [of vegetation].[20]

[1] That is, after the initial address warning mankind of the Convulsion of the Hour and exposing those who dispute concerning God without knowledge (cf. 22: 1–3), the discourse returns to them with a rational demonstration (istidlāl) of the possibility of Resurrection, directing their attention to what, from the human perspective, appears greater: the first creation. The argument proceeds from the more remarkable instance to what is more readily conceivable: if origination after non-existence is acknowledged, then restoration after prior existence can hardly be denied. This comparison concerns human reasoning; neither the first creation nor Resurrection presents any difficulty to God. As the Exalted says: “Were We then wearied by the first creation? Rather, they are in confusion regarding a new creation” (50: 15). The One Who originated the human being from dust, then from a drop of fluid, and fashioned him through successive stages of creation is surely Able to bring him forth again after death and bodily dissolution (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] Rayb indicates doubt, often accompanied by apprehension, suspicion, or inward unease. Ibn Fāris gives its fundamental sense as doubt, sometimes attended by fear; Ibn al-Hāʾim explains it as doubt accompanied by suspicion concerning what is doubted; and al-Iṣfahānī relates it to forming an uncertain supposition about something. al-Zamakhsharī particularly draws attention to its psychological force: rībah is the unease and disturbance that such doubt produces within the soul. The expression rābanī al-shayÒu means “a thing caused me misgiving” (cf. Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān).
 [3] That is, mankind’s original creation through their father Adam (عليه السلام), whom God created from dust (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī). al-Shinqīṭī explains: “The sound interpretation of His creating mankind from dust is that He created their father, Adam, from it, then created his spouse from him, and from the two of them brought forth their progeny through procreation. As the Exalted says: ‘Indeed, the likeness of ʿĪsā in the sight of Allah is as the likeness of Adam: He created him from dust’ (3: 59). Since their original root is from dust, their creation is ascribed to dust, for the branches follow the root.” (Aḍwāʾ al-Bayān). al-Rāzī also mentions another explanation, namely that the substances from which human beings are generated ultimately derive through nourishment from the Earth. al-Shinqīṭī, however, does not regard this as the intended meaning here.
 [4] Nuṭfah is a small quantity or drop of seminal fluid, here referring to the reproductive fluid from which human creation proceeds (cf. al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, Abīū al-Suʿīūd, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī). As the Exalted says: “Was he not a drop of semen, emitted? *Then he became a clinging clot, then He fashioned and proportioned him, *then He made from him the two sexes, male and female. Is not that One Able to give life to the dead?” (75: 37–40)
 [5] ʿAlaqah refers to a clot or clinging substance. The root ʿ-l-q denotes attachment or the clinging of one thing to another (cf. Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Qurṭubī, Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān). Here it refers to the stage in which the developing human is a clot-like substance attached to the mother’s womb. Classical exegetes variously describe it as congealed blood, fresh blood, or intensely red blood (cf. al-Qurṭubī, Abīū al-Suʿīūd, al-Saʿdī).
 [6] Muḍghah: a small piece of flesh, of the size that may be chewed; its root derives from maḍgh, meaning to chew (cf. al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt).
 [7] Exegetes have differed regarding the precise meaning of mukhallaqah (formed) and ghayr mukhallaqah (unformed). al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, who attributes it to the majority, and al-Saʿdī hold that mukhallaqah means that which has been fully fashioned, while ghayr mukhallaqah refers to the miscarried foetus before completion of its formation. al-Ṭabarī maintains that once the drop has become a muḍghah, no stage remains before it becomes a well-proportioned human except that of shaping; thus, the phrase signifies either a fully formed creation or a lump expelled before being shaped or before the spirit is breathed into it. al-Wāḥidī supports this view with the report of Ibn Masʿīūd concerning the angel who asks whether the drop is formed or unformed, and whose determination precedes the recording of sex, provision, lifespan, and ultimate destiny. al-Shinqīṭī objects that the context addresses mankind generally, and therefore both descriptions must pertain to those who become human beings; otherwise, inconsistency would arise. He further argues that the clause “We cause to settle in the wombs what We will until a fixed term” does not necessarily imply miscarriage, for settlement varies by Divine Will. al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, and al-Shinqīṭī interpret the phrase as indicating variation within the muḍghah itself: some embryos develop fully and free of defect, others incompletely or irregularly. This diversity accounts for differences among people in form, stature, and constitution. al-Rāzī argues that since the address is to mankind, the descriptions must apply to those who become human beings. Muḥyī al-Dīn Zādah similarly prefers this interpretation, noting that the verbal form suggests multiplicity and diversification in creation. Ibn ʿĀshīūr concludes that mukhallaqah wa ghayr mukhallaqah are attributes of the muḍghah, denoting successive developmental states. Unlike the nuṭfah and the ʿalaqah, the muḍghah admits differentiation in form. As such, both descriptions pertain to stages of embryonic development rather than to miscarriage.
 [8] The object of “make clear” is left unstated in the Arabic, allowing the expression to encompass what these successive stages of creation demonstrate: God’s Power and Wisdom, and His Ability to resurrect the dead (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [9] That is, so that God Almighty may make clear to mankind the origin of their creation and demonstrate His Power to them (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī). Exegetes differ regarding the syntactic attachment and implied object of li-nubayyina lakum (“so that We may make clear to you”). al-Ṭabarī relates it to the distinction between the formed and unformed muḍghah, understanding the clause as explaining why the two states are mentioned. Others, including Abīū Ḥayyān, Abīū al-Suʿīūd, al-Alīūsī and al-Shinqīṭī, connect it to khalaqnākum (“We created you”), taking the successive stages of creation as a general demonstration of Divine Power. Ibn Juzayy connects it to an implied verb, in the sense: “We mentioned this so that We may make clear to you.” al-Zajjāj records both this interpretation and the possibility that it is connected directly to “We created you”. Because the object of nubayyina is left unstated, some exegetes understand the expression broadly as encompassing the manner of human creation, Divine Power and Wisdom, and the truth of the Resurrection.
 [10] God Almighty causes whatever He Wills to remain in the wombs until the appointed term of birth (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Saʿdī). The duration of gestation varies according to Divine Will: some remain for shorter periods and others for longer, while other pregnancies end before development is complete.
 [11] al-Biqāʿī observes: “Then We bring you forth as a child, that is, in the state of infancy, small in stature, weak in body, hearing, sight, and all other faculties, lest the size and weight of your bodies endanger your mothers.”
 [12] ashuddakum (“your full strength”) denotes the stage of youthful vigour at which one’s faculties reach full strength. The word derives from the root sh-d-d, which conveys strength, firmness, and intensity. The same root is also associated with elevation, as in shadd al-nahār, the rising of the day towards its height (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-QurÒān; al-Azharī, Tahdhīb al-Lughah; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; Abīū Ḥayyān, al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān; al-Kafawī, al-Kulliyyāt; Ibn ʿĀshīūr). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah explains that opinions concerning al-ashudd range from eighteen to thirty years, thirty-two, thirty-six, forty, or forty-five. The term is used in more than one sense: the ashudd of a human being in general is not necessarily the same as the ashudd of an orphan, where it may refer to puberty. In this aya, he considers both senses possible. Elsewhere, commenting on Aya 12: 22, al-Samʿānī explains: “Most authorities hold that al-ashudd is reached at thirty-three years, when youthful strength attains its culmination.”
 [13] Ardhal al-ʿumur (“the lowest stage of life”) refers to extreme decrepitude and senility, in which previously acquired strength and knowledge decline; it does not describe old age in every person. Ardhal in relation to anything specifies that which is base, inferior, and of the poorest quality (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; Ibn Manẓīūr, Lisān al-ʿArab).
 [14] Among people are those who die before reaching their full strength; and among them are those whose death is deferred until they are returned to the most abject stage of life, becoming weak in body and mind, devoid of knowledge and understanding, after once having been strong and possessed of awareness and insight (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, al-Shawkānī, al-Saʿdī): “Allah is the One Who created you from weakness, then after weakness made strength, then after strength made weakness and grey hair. He creates whatever He wills, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful” (30: 54).
 [15] Here, God Almighty sets forth a second observable and decisive proof of the Resurrection (cf. al-Shinqīṭī).
 [16] Hāmidah: barren and lifeless, with no vegetation growing upon it. The root h-m-d denotes subsiding, dying away, or becoming still, as when a fire is extinguished or vegetation withers (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb).
 [17] It has been said that what is meant by it is rain from the sky (cf. al-Ṭabarī). It has also been said that it is more general than that, whether from rain, rivers, springs, or water drawn by waterwheels; this has been preferred by Abīū Ḥayyān and al-Shinqīṭī.
 [18] al-Wāḥidī states that the exegetes understand its “stirring” to mean the movement of the earth as vegetation emerges after water descends upon it. As plants spring forth, the earth rises, and this rise constitutes its movement. Accordingly, His saying “and it swells” signifies that it rises and increases. Abīū Ḥayyān explains that its stirring refers to the loosening of the earth and the disturbance of some of its parts as vegetation begins to grow. al-Qurṭubī likewise explains that the earth stirs with vegetation because plants cannot emerge without subtly displacing parts of the soil from one another. The stirring is therefore attributed to the earth metaphorically. al-Samʿānī notes that the aya may involve reordering, yielding the sense “it swells and stirs”. It is also said that “it stirs” refers to the vegetation, while rabat means “it rose”; the feminine verbal forms are used because the earth has been mentioned. al-Shinqīṭī explains that its stirring means its movement with vegetation: since the vegetation grows within the earth and remains attached to it, its movement is spoken of as though it were the movement of the earth itself, a recognised mode of Arabic expression.
 [19] Ibn ʿĀshīūr explains that rabat (“and it swells”) means that the earth undergoes rubuww, that is, increase. The expression rabā yarbīū rubuwwan means that something increases. Here it refers to the swelling of the earth as plants and trees break forth. al-Shinqīṭī considers the more apparent interpretation to be that the vegetation, because it grows within and remains attached to the earth, appears as though it were an increase in the earth itself.
 [20] Zawj bahīj means a beautiful and delightful kind of vegetation. Bahīj carries the sense of mubhij, something pleasing and beautiful in appearance, such that the eye delights in beholding it. It derives from bahjah, the beauty and freshness of a thing. The root z-w-j denotes the association or pairing of one thing with another, while zawj may consequently suggest a kind or variety (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Wāḥidī, al-Basīṭ): “And He sent down for you water from the sky; then We caused gardens full of delight to grow thereby, whose trees you could never have caused to grow” (27: 60).
[1]That is because Allah is the Truth,[2] and that He gives life to the dead, and because He is Powerful over all things.

[1] Having established the two preceding proofs, the stages of human creation and the revival of the lifeless earth, God, Glorified be He, then sets forth the conclusions that necessarily follow from them and are intended to be established by those proofs (cf. al-Rāzī, Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb).
 [2] What has been described to people concerning the stages of their creation and the revival of the land with water after its death is so that they may know that God is the Truth, about Whom there can be no doubt (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Shawkānī). He Alone deserves to be worshipped; worshipping Him is true, while worshipping anything besides Him is false (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Saʿdī).
And [you may realise] that the Hour is coming, no doubt is there in it, and because Allah shall raise those who are in the graves.[1]

[1] From the opening of the sura through His Words: “and because Allah shall raise those who are in the graves” (22: 7), the discourse presents a striking example of what classical rhetoricians call al-madhhab al-kalāmī, the dialectical mode of argumentation, in which sound conclusions are derived from established premises. al-Suyīūṭī observes that these ayas yield five conclusions from ten premises, drawing together mass-transmitted reports and observable Signs. First, the Convulsion of the Hour is reported with emphatic certainty. The report is conveyed by the Messenger (ﷺ), whose truthfulness is established, from God, Whose Power is established, and has reached the community through mass transmission. So, it is true, and no one can truthfully disclose what is yet to come except the One Who is the Truth: “That is because Allah is the Truth” (22: 6). Second, the description of the terrors of the Hour presupposes that the dead will be brought back to life to witness them. Giving life to the dead is, moreover, necessarily encompassed by God’s Power over all things: “and that He gives life to the dead” (22: 6). Third, the threat against those who follow rebellious devils and dispute concerning God without knowledge culminates in their being guided to the Punishment of the Blaze. The certain execution of such requital can belong only to One Whose Power encompasses all things: “and because He is Powerful over all things” (22: 6). Fourth, the argument anchors the Unseen in what can be observed. God creates the human being through successive stages, from dust, to a drop of fluid, to a clinging clot, to a morsel of flesh, formed and unformed, then brings life to completion and finally causes death. Likewise, He revives barren earth with rain until it stirs, swells, and brings forth vegetation. What is visibly witnessed therefore confirms what is promised concerning restoration after death: “And [you may realise] that the Hour is coming, no doubt is there in it” (22: 7). Fifth, the coming of the Hour entails the resurrection of the dead for recompense. The Hour cannot fulfil its purpose of judgement unless those in the graves are raised: “and because Allah shall raise those who are in the graves” (22: 7) (cf. al-Suyīūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlīūm al-Qur’ān; al-Suyīūṭī, Muʿtarak al-Aqrān fī Iʿjāz al-Qur’ān, 1: 346; Darwīsh, Iʿrāb al-Qur’ān wa Bayānuh, 6: 397–398).
[1]And among people is one who disputes concerning Allah[2] without knowledge,[3] nor guidance,[4] nor an illuminating Book,[5]

[1] This clause is coordinated with the sentence beginning with the address in Aya 5, just as Aya 3 is coordinated with the opening address in Aya 1. If people are in doubt about the Resurrection, the clear proofs that follow are intended to remove that doubt; people then divide between those convinced by these pieces of evidence and those who persist in disputation. The interposed statement, “no doubt is there in it”, categorically negates the legitimacy of any doubt concerning the Hour. On Ibn ʿĀshīūr’s principal interpretation, the disputers in Aya 8 are the same obstinate leaders of Association already described in Aya 3, but now portrayed after the warning of the Hour and after the proofs of Resurrection have been set forth. Their disputation proceeds without knowledge, guidance, or an illuminating Book, that is, without any revealed Scripture or Divine law that could support their argument. It is further marked by an arrogant refusal to acknowledge the proof and a deliberate desire to mislead others from the way of God. Ibn ʿĀshīūr also records an alternative interpretation according to which Aya 3 describes the followers who imitate the Associators, while Aya 8 describes the leaders whom they follow (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] That is, concerning God, particularly His Oneness and exclusive right to be worshipped, His Power to resurrect the dead, and the Truth He has revealed (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Shawkānī, al-Saʿdī).
 [3] Some hold that “knowledge” (ʿilm) here refers to immediate or necessary knowledge apprehended without reflection or inference. On this interpretation, the three expressions form a comprehensive division of the possible sources of knowledge: ʿilm denotes immediate or necessary knowledge, hudā specifies knowledge reached through rational investigation and inference, and kitāb munīr (“an illuminating Book”) points to knowledge received through Divine revelation. The disputant therefore possesses neither immediate certainty, rational proof, nor revealed guidance (cf. al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Shinqīṭī).
 [4] He disputes about God on the basis of nothing but his own opinion and whim, without any sound proof to guide him to what is right (cf. al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Shawkānī, al-Saʿdī).
 [5] Kitāb munīr is an illuminating Divine Book, clear in its proofs and shedding light upon the Truth, by which a person may be rightly guided and his argument grounded in authoritative revelation (cf. al-Nasafī, Abīū al-Suʿīūd, al-Alīūsī, al-Shinqīṭī).

turning his side [and neck in arrogance],[1] to lead [others] astray[2] from the way of Allah. For him there is disgrace in this world;[3] and on the Day of Judgement, We shall make him taste the Punishment of the Burning [Fire].

[1] Thāniya ʿiṭfihi depicts him twisting his neck or turning his side away in haughty rejection. The root th-n-y fundamentally denotes doubling or folding, and thus bending or turning. ʿIṭf signifies the side of the body; a person’s two ʿiṭfs are the two sides extending from the head to the hips. It may therefore describe the bending of the neck, the turning away of one’s side, or, figuratively, an arrogant rejection of the Truth. al-Ṭabarī regards these interpretations as closely related expressions of the same haughty turning away (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; al-Baghawī; al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī).
 [2] There are two canonical readings of this expression. The majority read li-yuḍilla (“to lead others astray”), while Ibn Kathīr, Abīū ʿAmr, and Ruways from Yaʿqīūb read li-yaḍilla (“to go astray”). On the latter reading, some commentators understand the lām as lām al-ʿāqibah, indicating the outcome of his conduct rather than an intention on his part: he disputes arrogantly and consequently goes astray (cf. Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rasʿanī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Alīūsī). On the majority reading, li-yuḍilla, the lām may be understood as lām al-taʿlīl, expressing purpose. Ibn ʿĀshīūr takes it as describing the disputant’s own motive: he argues arrogantly to lead others astray from the way of God and prevent them from following the Truth. al-Shinqīṭī gives the construction a different explanation. He rejects treating such usages merely as lām al-ʿāqibah and understands the purpose from the standpoint of Divine decree and Wisdom: God decrees the person’s conduct such that he becomes both astray himself and one who leads others astray, even where such an outcome is not the conscious purpose of the immediate human agent (cf. al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī).
 [3] Exegetes differ concerning what constitutes the worldly khizy (“disgrace”) mentioned here. A substantial strand understands it as concrete historical humiliation, including killing, abasement, defeat, and captivity at the hands of the Believers. al-Ṭabarī explains it as the killing, abasement, and humiliation that befell those who disputed concerning God without knowledge. Ibn ʿĀshīūr likewise interprets it as worldly abasement manifested in killing and capture, applying it particularly to Abīū Jahl and al-Naḍr Ibn al-Ḥārith. Abīū Jahl was struck down at Badr by two young Anṣārīs, the sons of ʿAfrāʾ, after which ʿAbd Allāh Ibn Masʿīūd killed him; al-Naḍr was captured at Badr and later executed at al-Uthayl near Madinah. Since, in Ibn ʿĀshīūr’s view, this aya was certainly revealed in Makkah, he regards the promised worldly disgrace as a disclosure of the Unseen subsequently fulfilled at Badr, and thus as one of the Qur’an’s miraculous signs. A similar historical application is reported from Muqātil, Makkī, al-Samʿānī, al-Baghawī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Khāzin, and Ibn Jurayj. al-Māturīdī reports that many exegetes applied the aya specifically to al-Naḍr Ibn al-Ḥārith, while also recording al-Ḥasan’s broader interpretation applying it to the Deniers generally. al-Qurṭubī gives another sense of khizy: enduring shame and infamous remembrance, whereby such people remain publicly branded with disgrace. He also records the killing of al-Naḍr after Badr as another interpretation. More broadly, the expression may encompass the recurring worldly exposure, refutation, defeat, hatred, and humiliation that befall arrogant leaders who turn others away from God’s Way.
That is for what your hands have sent forth,[1] and because Allah is never [in the least] unjust to His servants.[2]

[1] That is, what his own hands have sent forth during his worldly life, namely his Denial and acts of disobedience (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Shinqīṭī).
 [2] The intensive form ẓallām (“extremely unjust”) is used here, although merely negating an intensive form does not, by itself, necessarily negate the underlying quality altogether. In this regard, exegetes have offered several explanations for its use. First, the intensive force corresponds to the multitude of servants. If even the slightest injustice were done to every servant, the aggregate would amount to immense injustice. Accordingly, negating ẓallām in relation to the countless multitude of servants amounts to negating every degree of injustice towards each one of them. God is exalted above wronging anyone in the least (cf. al-Bayḍāwī, Abīū al-Suʿīūd, al-Shinqīṭī, on 41: 46). Second, external and contextual evidence makes clear that what is intended is the complete negation of injustice. Numerous ayas explicitly establish this, such as: “Surely Allah does not wrong people in anything, but people wrong themselves” (10: 44). The intensive negation is therefore understood in the light of these unequivocal statements (cf. al-Shinqīṭī, on 41: 46). Third, the severity of God’s Punishment itself helps explain the intensive form. Were such tremendous Punishment inflicted upon those who did not deserve it through their Denial and acts of disobedience, that would constitute extreme injustice. Infinitely exalted is He above that (cf. al-Shinqīṭī, on 41: 46). Fourth, the pattern faʿʿāl may sometimes function attributively rather than intensively, conveying the sense of possessing or being characterised by a quality, much as a nisbah yāʾ does. On this interpretation, “Allah is not ẓallām to the servants” means that He is not characterised by injustice in any respect (cf. al-Shinqīṭī, on 41: 46). al-Biqāʿī explains: “Not in the least unjust (laysa bi-ẓallām), that is, He commits no injustice at all against His servants. For if He were to leave you without such requital, then by your own ordinary standards, it would count as injustice in two respects: first, because it would place the one who does good on a par with the one who does evil; and second, because it would fail to vindicate those who opposed you for His sake and whom you harmed on His account.”

[1]And among people is he who worships Allah upon an edge;[2] if good befalls him, he is reassured by it, but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face,[3] losing this worldly life and the Hereafter[4]—that is the manifest loss.

[1] After the state of those who openly profess Association and dispute in its defence has been clarified, the discourse turns to another group: the wavering ones, who neither embrace Islam with firm conviction in its truth nor turn away from it altogether. Rather, they enter it while inwardly weighing it against their former religion. If some good befalls them, they take this as evidence that Islam is true and that their former gods are powerless; but if some passing worldly harm befalls them through ordinary causes, they grow resentful and cast Islam off, imagining that their former gods have afflicted them in retaliation for their abandonment of those gods’ worship (cf. al-Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). Ibn ʿAbbās (رضي الله عنهما) said, commenting on His Words: “And among people is he who worships Allah upon an edge”: “A man would come to Madinah, and if his wife gave birth to a son and his mares foaled, he would say, ‘This is a good religion.’ But if his wife did not give birth and his mares did not foal, he would say, ‘This is an evil religion!’” (al-Bukhārī: 4742).
 [2] ʿAlā ḥarf (“upon an edge”) denotes doubt and instability. Faith has not taken firm root in his heart; rather, he remains in doubt, unease, and hesitation concerning the religion of God (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Saʿdī). Most exegetes understand the expression through the image of someone standing precariously on the edge of a mountain or wall, without firm footing and liable to slip. It thus portrays one who worships God without certainty, steadfastness, or inward assurance (cf. al-Wāḥidī). It has also been said that ḥarf here means a condition, namely that he worships God conditionally, remaining committed only so long as some worldly good, such as ease, health, or prosperity, befalls him (cf. al-Shawkānī).
 [3] Inqalaba ʿalā wajhihi (“turns back on his face”) is understood by most exegetes as returning to his former state of Denial when adversity befalls him (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Saʿdī). Ibn Taymiyyah likens him to one standing on the edge of a valley: if good befalls him, he remains at ease, but if tried, he falls headlong. Ibn ʿĀshīūr further argues that “he turns on his face” preserves the vivid image of being overturned and falling headlong, rather than merely turning back, i.e. the expression completes the earlier image of one standing precariously on an edge. Though inqilāb may figuratively symbolize returning whence one came, Ibn ʿĀshīūr considers that sense less fitting here, since retreat is more naturally expressed in the Qur’an by “turning on one’s heels” (2: 143). A similar type is described in the Qur’an: “And among the people is he who says, ‘We Believe in Allah,’ but when he is harmed for Allah’s sake, he takes the trial of people to be like Allah’s Punishment. Yet if victory comes from your Lord, they will surely say, ‘Indeed, we were with you.’ Is not Allah best aware of what lies within the breasts of all beings? And Allah will surely make known those who Believe, and He will surely make known the hypocrites” (29: 10-11). Jābir Ibn ʿAbdillāh (رضي الله عنهما) relates that a Bedouin pledged allegiance to The Prophet (ﷺ) to adhere to Islam. When he was afflicted by fever in Madinah, he asked The Prophet (ﷺ) to release him from his pledge. He made the request three times in all, and the Prophet refused each time. When the Bedouin departed, The Prophet (ﷺ) said: “Madinah is like a furnace: it expels its impurity, and its pure part shines forth” (al-Bukhārī: 7211; Muslim: 1383). The report illustrates a commitment marked by unsteadfastness under trial, although it need not imply that the Bedouin had renounced Islam.
 [4] He who turns back in this manner loses the good of this worldly life, for he fails to obtain what he sought therein and is deprived of inner reassurance and the esteem and fellowship of the Muslims. He also loses the good of the Hereafter by entering the Fire and being denied Paradise (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Saʿdī).
He invokes, apart from Allah, that which neither harms him nor benefits him.[1] That is the misguidance far removed [from the Truth].

[1] That is, the one who turns away from the religion of God calls upon deities apart from God that possess, in themselves, no power whatsoever either to harm or benefit him (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Shinqīṭī).
He calls one whose harm is nearer than his benefit.[1] How wretched a patron, and how wretched an intimate companion![2]

[1] It is as though it were said: he calls upon not merely that which cannot harm him, but that through whose worship harm comes to him. This harm does not arise from any power possessed by the false deity itself; rather, worshipping it harms him in this worldly life through futile reliance upon it, and in the Hereafter through punishment (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] How wretched is such an object of worship as a protector, and how wretched as a companion; it neither aids its worshipper nor brings him any benefit (cf. al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī).
[1]Indeed, Allah admits[2] those who Believe and do righteous deeds into Gardens beneath which rivers flow—indeed, Allah does whatever He Wills.[3]

[1] The aya contrasts the worship and fate of the true Believers with those previously described. al-Rāzī contrasts both their worship and their objects of worship: the worship of the wavering is unsound, and their objects of worship can neither harm nor benefit them, whereas the Believers’ worship is true and God grants them the greatest benefit, Paradise. al-Saʿdī likewise distinguishes merely nominal faith from true Faith confirmed by righteous deeds. Ibn Juzayy observes that, after showing the inability of idols to benefit their worshippers, the aya shows that God grants His worshippers the greatest benefit, admission into Paradise. Ibn ʿĀshīūr further notes that the aya stands in contrast to the earlier threats of Punishment and loss in Ayas 9 and 11, while the concluding statement, “Indeed, Allah does whatever He Wills”, gives the general explanation for the differing outcomes of people in this worldly life and the Hereafter (cf. al-Rāzī, al-Saʿdī, Ibn Juzayy, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] That is, on the Day of Judgement (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Abīū al-Suʿīūd, al-Shawkānī, al-Saʿdī).
 [3] That is, God does whatever He Wills. He grants honour to the obedient and humiliation to the disobedient, rewards or punishes as He Wills, and none can prevent or oppose Him. He decrees for His creation whatever He Wills of felicity and wretchedness, including admitting the Believers into Paradise (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Samarqandī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī).

[1] Whoever thinks that Allah will never aid him in this world and the Hereafter, let him then stretch a means [of a rope][2] up to the sky, then cut [himself] off, and then let him see whether his scheming will indeed remove that which enrages him.

[1] The pronoun in “aid him” has been understood in two principal ways. Most exegetes, as al-Wāḥidī notes, take it to refer to The Prophet (ﷺ): whoever thinks that God will not aid His Messenger in this worldly life and the Hereafter may do whatever his rage drives him to do, for he cannot prevent that promised aid. al-Shinqīṭī regards this as the clearest interpretation and summarises its force as: let such people die in their rage, for God will certainly aid him (cf. al-Wāḥidī, al-Shinqīṭī). Ibn Juzayy, however, prefers the pronoun as referring to the wavering person described earlier, who worships God “upon an edge”. On this reading, if trial causes him to despair of God’s aid, relief, or provision, let him destroy himself in rage and see whether that alters anything. Ibn ʿĀshīūr likewise favours this interpretation in his principal discussion, while also acknowledging The Prophet (ﷺ) as another possible referent (cf. Ibn Juzayy, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). The image itself has also been understood in different ways. On the interpretation that “the sky” means the ceiling of one’s house, the command is a taunting rebuke: let him hang himself and choke in his rage. al-Zamakhsharī explains that “cut off” may denote choking because the breath is cut off, and that the act is called “scheming” either because it is the utmost he can do or as a mockery, since he harms only himself. Ibn ʿĀshīūr, taking “the sky” literally, explains the command as one of incapacity: let him stretch a rope to the sky and cut it, if he can, yet none of this will remove his rage. On either interpretation, the hostile or despairing person’s rage harms only himself and cannot prevent what God has Willed (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Baghawī, Ibn Juzayy, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī).
 [2] Bi-sabab means “by means of a rope”. More generally, sabab points to any means by which something is reached. al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī explains that the word depicts a rope used for climbing and, by extension, any means through which an end is attained. Ibn Fāris tentatively attributes the rope sense to length and extension (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; al-Ṭabarī, al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān).
[1]And thus, We have sent it (the Qur’an) down as clear Signs, [2]and that Allah guides whom He Wills.

[1] After the preceding ayas have set out with unmistakable clarity the different ways people respond to the call of Islam, this aya draws attention to the clarity of the Revelation itself. God has sent it down as clear Signs, plain in both wording and meaning and leaving no room for ambiguity (cf. Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). Its revelation in this clear form serves the purpose of guidance, for God guides through the Qur’an whom He Wills (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] The clause “and that Allah guides whom He Wills” explains the purpose of sending the Qur’an down as clear Signs: God has revealed it in this lucid form so that through it He guides whom He Wills to the Truth. The Qur’an is clear in itself, plain in its wording and meaning, and directs people towards what is beneficial, yet guidance remains entirely in God’s Hand. Those whom He Wills to guide take it as light and guidance, while those whom He does not Will to guide gain no benefit from it, and it becomes a proof against them (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, Ibn Juzayy, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).

[1]Indeed, those who Believe, and those who are Jews, and the ṢābiÒīn,[2] and the Christians, and the Magians,[3] and those who Associate others with Allah, Allah shall indeed judge decisively between them on the Day of Resurrection—verily, Allah is Witness over all things.[4]

[1] This aya sums up the preceding passage. After the preceding ayas have described those who waver in accepting Islam, the question naturally arises concerning the different religious communities, each claiming to possess the Truth while regarding the others as false and disputing with them. The aya therefore states that God will judge between them on the Day of Judgement concerning all that they differed over, since their arguments in this worldly life proved of no benefit in resolving their disagreements. This consigning of judgement to God also carries an implied assertion of confidence, for one entrusts the final decision to Him in this manner only when confident that one’s position is true (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] ṢābiÒīn (“Sabians”) is the accusative plural of ṢābiÒ. The root ṣ-b-Ò refers to coming out or emerging, and the Arabs used ṣābiÒ for someone who left one religion for another; the same root is used for the stars when they emerge or rise (cf. Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Wāḥidī, al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; al-Qurṭubī, Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān). Exegetes and other Muslim scholars differed considerably over the precise identity of the Sabians. They were not understood as a single uniform group; Ibn al-Qayyim, for example, distinguishes Ḥanīf ṢābiÒīūn, Associating ṢābiÒīūn, philosophical ṢābiÒīūn, and others bearing the designation (cf. Ibn al-Qayyim, Ighāthat al-Lahfān; Ibn Kathīr). The term therefore should not be restricted to one particular later religious community. The Sabians are mentioned three times in the Qur’an. In Ayas 2: 62 and 5: 69, they occur among communities in connection with Belief in God, the Last Day, and righteous deeds, while in Aya 22: 17 they appear among the religious communities between whom God will judge on the Day of Judgement. Classical exegetes differ over the historical and legal scope of the promise in 2: 62 and 5: 69; as a result, it should not be reduced to the general claim that communal labels alone are irrelevant to salvation (cf. al-Ṭabarī).
 [3] The Magians (al-Majīūs) are generally identified with the Zoroastrians, particularly the Iranian Zoroastrian communities known to the late antique and early Islamic worlds. Although the precise historical relationship between the ancient Magi and early Zoroastrianism remains debated, al-Majīūs became the common Arabic designation for Zoroastrians. Unlike the Sabians, whose precise identity is considerably more disputed, the Magians, thus, represent a more readily identifiable historical religious community. In this aya, nonetheless, they are mentioned as one of the religious communities between whom God will judge on the Day of Judgement (cf. al-Ṭabarī).
 [4] That is, God is Witness over all their deeds, movements, and words; nothing whatsoever is hidden from Him (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr).

[1]Do you not see [2] that to Allah prostrates whoever is in the Heavens and whoever is on Earth, and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the moving creatures,[3] and a multitude of people?[4] Yet a multitude have truly deserved the Punishment.[5] And whoever Allah abases has none to honour him[6]—verily, Allah does whatever He Wills.[7]

[1] After the previous aya has stated that God will judge between the various religious communities on the Day of Judgement, this aya shows how unfitting such disagreement is in a universe wholly subject to His Power. al-Marāghī observes that all the higher and lower realms, great and small, are subjected to God’s Might and governed by His Power, which should have sufficed to lead people away from such disagreement. The aya also opens a fresh proof of God’s exclusive Divinity: the state of all creation, rational and otherwise, bears witness that He Alone is worthy of worship (cf. al-Marāghī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). This universal submission, however, is not identical in every case. All creation necessarily submits to God’s Power, governance, and Will, while many human beings additionally prostrate to Him willingly in worship. Others refuse such devotional submission and thereby become deserving of Punishment (cf. al-Marāghī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] The address in “Do you not see” may be understood generally, as directed to everyone capable of understanding and reflecting, or specifically to the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), with others included by implication. Here tarā denotes perception by the heart and intellect, in the sense of “Do you not know or consider?”, rather than ordinary visual observation (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Abīū al-Suʿīūd, al-Shawkānī, al-Alīūsī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [3] The prostration of these creatures is according to what befits each of them. Exegetes distinguish between a general prostration of subjection to God’s Lordship, Power, and decree, which encompasses all creation, and the willing devotional prostration of those who worship Him. Hence, even those human beings who refuse to prostrate willingly remain subject to His Power and governance, while the Believers prostrate to Him willingly in worship. Ibn al-Qayyim explicitly distinguishes this general prostration from the special prostration mentioned here, where “many people” willingly prostrate to God (cf. Ibn al-Qayyim, Madārij al-Sālikīn). Some exegetes also explain the prostration of created things through the visible movement of their shadows as the sun moves across the sky. al-Ṭabarī, for example, interprets the changing shadows of these creatures as a form of their prostration. The underlying general sense is submission to God’s Command and Power, while the precise manner of each creature’s prostration befits its nature (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn al-Qayyim, Madārij al-Sālikīn; Ibn Taymiyyah, Majmīūʿ al-Fatāwā; Ibn Kathīr, al-Shawkānī, al-Samʿānī). “To ‘Allah’ prostrates ˹all˺ who are in the Heavens and Earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shades early and late in the day!” (13: 15). “Have they not considered how the shadows of everything Allah has created incline to the right and the left ˹as the sun moves˺, prostrating to Allah in a state of abject humility? And to Allah prostrates whatever is in the Heavens and whatever is on Earth of moving creatures, and the angels ˹as well˺; they do not wax arrogant!” (16: 48–49).
 [4] This refers to the Believers, who prostrate to God willingly, by choice, and as an act of worship (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr).
 [5] On one widely held interpretation, this refers to the Deniers, upon whom God’s Punishment has become due because they refuse to prostrate to Him voluntarily as an act of worship (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr). Mujāhid, on the other hand, understands them as still included among those who “prostrate”, in that their shadows prostrate to God even though Punishment has become due upon them because of their Denial (cf. al-Ṭabarī).
 [6] That is, God has abased them by making Punishment due upon them, so they will find none to honour them through support or intercession (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr). Disobedience causes a servant to become lowly in the sight of his Lord. Ibn al-Qayyim relates from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: “They became lowly in His sight, so they disobeyed Him; had they been dear to Him, He would have protected them.” Ibn al-Qayyim adds that when God abases a servant, no one can truly honour him. Even if people outwardly show him respect because they need him or fear his harm, inwardly they regard him with contempt (cf. Ibn al-Qayyim, al-Jawāb al-Kāfī, “Faṣl: Hawān al-ʿāṣī ʿalā rabbih”).
 [7] That is, God does whatever He Wills among His creation: He grants happiness and honour to whom He Wills, and decrees wretchedness and humiliation for whom He Wills. The creation is His creation, and the Command is His (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī).
[1]These are two adversaries who have disputed concerning their Lord. As for those who Denied, garments of Fire are cut out for them;[2] scalding water[3] is poured from above their heads.

[1] “These are two adversaries” refers broadly to the Believers and the Deniers, who disputed concerning their Lord, His Oneness, and His religion. The Believers seek to support God’s religion and make His Word supreme, while the Deniers seek to extinguish the light of Faith, suppress the Truth, and make falsehood prevail (cf. Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). The aya was also applied to the six men who came forth for single combat at Badr, three Companions against three Qurayshī opponents. Qays Ibn ʿAbbād reported: “I heard Abīū Dharr (رضي الله عنه) swear that ‘These are two adversaries who have disputed concerning their Lord’ was revealed concerning those who came forth for single combat on the Day of Badr: Ḥamzah, ʿAlī, and ʿUbaydah Ibn al-Ḥārith on one side, and ʿUtbah and Shaybah, the sons of Rabīʿah, and al-Walīd Ibn ʿUtbah on the other” (al-Bukhārī: 4743; Muslim: 3033).
 [2] This means that the Deniers will be clothed in garments of Fire, so that the Punishment envelops their bodies completely (cf. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn Juzayy, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī): “And you shall see the criminals bound on that Day in shackles; *their vestures are of tar and the Fire covers their faces!” (14: 49-50).
 [3] al-Ḥamīm is scalding water of intense heat. The root ḥ-m-m stands for heat (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt): “Seize him and drag him into the midst of Hellfire! *Then pour over his head from the Punishment of scalding water!” (44: 47-48).
With it, whatever is in their bellies,[1] as well as their skins,[2] is melted.

[1] “With it” refers to the scalding water poured over the heads of the Deniers. It melts what is within their bellies, their flesh, fat, and entrails, as well as their skins (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Baghawī, al-Saʿdī).
 [2] The apparent sense is that the scalding water melts their skins just as it melts what is within their bellies because of its intense heat. Some exegetes, however, understand “the skins” with an implied verb, meaning that their skins are burned or scorched by it (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Shinqīṭī).
[1]For them there are maces of iron.[2]

[1] In Hellfire, the angelic wardens will strike the Deniers with iron clubs, or hammers, and drive them back whenever they attempt to escape from the Fire (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī).
 [2] “Maces” translates maqāmiʿ: heavy iron clubs or hammers used for striking and subduing. The root q-m-ʿ carries the senses of subduing and abasing, and may also denote forcibly repelling or driving someone back (cf. Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Kafawī, al-Kulliyyāt).
Whenever they desire to get out of it out of anguish, they are returned therein,[1] and [it will be said]: “Taste the Punishment of the Burning Fire!”[2]

[1] “As for those who Denied, for them is the Fire of Hell: they will not be finished off so that they die, nor will any of its Punishment be lightened for them. Thus do We recompense every persistently ungrateful one. *And they cry out therein: ‘Our Lord, bring us out, we shall do righteousness other than what we used to do.’ Did We not grant you lives long enough for whoever would be mindful to be mindful? And the warner came to you. So taste, for the wrongdoers have no helper” (35: 36-37).
 [2] “As for those who defiantly disobeyed, their abode is the Fire. Whenever they desire to get out of it, they are returned to it, and it is said to them: ‘Taste the Punishment of the Fire which you used to deny’” (32: 20).

[1]Verily, Allah admits those who Believed and did righteous deeds into Gardens beneath which rivers flow. They are adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and with pearls,[2] and their clothing therein is silk.[3]

[1] After mentioning what awaits one of the two opposing parties, namely the Deniers, God follows this with what awaits the other, namely the Believers. Yet the passage is not merely joined to the previous one with “and”; rather, it opens independently, with inna and the Divine Name, drawing attention to the complete contrast between the two parties. The Believers’ entry into Gardens answers the Deniers’ repeated return to the Fire; their adornment with bracelets answers the scalding water poured over the Deniers’ heads; their silk clothing answers the Deniers’ garments of Fire; and, on Ibn ʿĀshīūr’s more contextually fitting interpretation, their being guided to places where they hear goodly speech answers the humiliating command: “Taste the Punishment of the Burning Fire!” (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] The readings of luÒluÒ allow more than one understanding of the adornment described here. In the accusative reading, luÒluÒan, read by Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Yaʿqīūb and others, the pearls constitute a separate adornment from the gold bracelets, such as pearl necklaces and the like. In the genitive reading, luÒluÒin, the expression may imply bracelets of pearl alongside bracelets of gold; it has also been understood as gold bracelets set with pearls. al-Qurṭubī regards bracelets made wholly of pearl as the more apparent sense of the aya (cf. al-Qurṭubī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). Abīū Hurayrah (رضي الله عنه) reported that The Prophet (ﷺ) said: “The adornment of the Believer will reach as far as his ablution reaches” (Muslim: 250).
 [3] Silk is mentioned because it was among the finest and most prized garments known, associated with exceptional luxury, beauty, and high rank. Its mention therefore evokes the honour, comfort, and splendour of the Believers’ clothing in the Gardens (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr). The Believers’ silk clothing in the Gardens also contrasts with its prohibition for men in this worldly life. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: “Do not wear silk, for whoever wears it in this worldly life will not wear it in the Hereafter” (Muslim: 2069). This is a severe warning concerning men who wear silk unlawfully, not women or those with a recognised exemption. He (ﷺ) also said concerning silk, brocade, and vessels of gold and silver: “They are for them in this worldly life, and for us in the Hereafter” (al-Bukhārī: 5426; Muslim: 2067). This does not mean that their use is lawful for the Deniers; rather, it contrasts their worldly enjoyment of such things with the Believers’ unrestricted enjoyment of them in the Hereafter.
They are guided to what is goodly of speech,[1] and they are guided to the Path of the All-Praiseworthy.[2]

[1] al-Ṭayyib min al-qawl (“what is goodly of speech”) has been understood in relation both to this worldly life and to the Hereafter. al-Ṭabarī principally understands it as God’s guiding the Believers in this worldly life to the testimony of Divine Oneness, lā ilāha illā Allāh. Other interpretations include the Qur’an, as reported from al-Suddī, prescribed remembrances, and every good and gracious word (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn Juzayy, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī, al-Shawkānī). Other exegetes emphasise the Hereafter. The Believers are guided to goodly speech in the Gardens, whether by being inspired to praise and glorify God or by being brought to places where they hear greetings of peace and other gracious words. al-Qurṭubī also records the interpretation that it refers to the glad tidings conveyed to them by God. Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀshīūr particularly favour the sense of being guided to where goodly speech is heard, since this forms a direct contrast with the humiliating words addressed to the people of the Fire: “Taste the Punishment of the Burning Fire!” The interpretations are complementary rather than mutually exclusive: the goodly word to which they were guided in this worldly life finds its blessed fulfilment in the speech of Paradise (cf. Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] “The Path of the All-Praiseworthy” is, on the principal interpretation, the Path of God, namely Islam, to which the Believers were guided in this worldly life, and which leads to His Pleasure. al-Ḥamīd is a Divine Attribute meaning the One Who is abundantly praised in His Essence, Names, Attributes, Acts, and Law (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). The expression has also been understood in relation to the Hereafter: God guides the Believers to the path of Paradise, where they praise Him for fulfilling His Promise and bestowing His favours. These two interpretations are complementary, for the path to which they were guided in this worldly life is the very path that leads them to Paradise in the Hereafter (cf. al-Qurṭubī). Grammatically, al-Ḥamīd may also describe the path itself, yielding the sense “the praiseworthy path”. On this reading, the construction is an instance of the described noun being annexed to its adjective. The path is praiseworthy in itself because it comprises Truth, wisdom, moderation, beneficial knowledge, and righteous action, and praiseworthy in its outcome because it leads those who follow it to God’s Pleasure and Paradise (cf. al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).

[1]Indeed, those who Denied and continue to bar from the Path of Allah and the Sacred Mosque, which We made for mankind,[2] equal therein are the resident and the visitor,[3] and whoever intends therein deviation through wrongdoing,[4] We shall make him taste a painful Punishment.

[1] After distinguishing between the Believers and the Deniers, and showing that the Believers’ bliss is grounded in their being “guided to the Path of the All-Praiseworthy”, the passage returns to the Deniers to expose the cause of their Punishment: their Denial and their persistent barring of others from God’s Path and from the Sacred Mosque. God’s Path here refers to Islam, while obstruction from the Sacred Mosque, though already included within that broader obstruction, is singled out because of its exceptional gravity and to introduce what follows concerning the sanctity of the Sacred House and the right of the Believers to worship there (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr). On Ibn ʿĀshīūr’s rhetorical reading, the past kafarīū (“Denied”) presents Denial as a defining characteristic of these people, while the present yaṣuddīūna (“bar”) points to their repeated and habitual conduct. Other grammarians, however, explain the tense relationship differently, taking it to describe their continuing state (cf. al-Rāzī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). Historically, the wording encompasses the Quraysh’s obstruction of The Prophet (ﷺ) and the Believers from the Sacred Mosque, while remaining general enough to include deliberate obstruction of Faith, worship, pilgrimage, or lawful access to the Sanctuary.
 [2] That is, those who Denied God’s Oneness and His Messengers and bar people from His religion and from the Sacred Mosque, which God has made for all people as a place of worship. Residents and visitors are alike in honouring its sanctity, worshipping therein, circumambulating the House, and performing its rites. So, the Quraysh possessed no exclusive right to prevent others from worshipping there (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, Maʿānī al-Qur’ān; al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī). “The Sacred Mosque” may refer specifically to the mosque surrounding the Kaʿbah or, more broadly, to the entire Sacred Precinct. Some exegetes also extended the equality of residents and visitors to the dwellings of Makkah, which gave rise to juristic disagreement concerning their ownership, sale, and rental; this, however, is a separate legal question. The Quraysh’s obstruction at al-Ḥudaybiyah provides a clear historical instance of the aya’s meaning: “They are the ones who Denied and barred you from the Sacred Mosque and the sacrificial offerings, detained from reaching their place of sacrifice” (48: 25). The parallel is strong, though it need not be treated as an uncontested occasion of revelation for Aya 22: 25.
 [3] “Equal therein are the resident and the visitor” means, on al-Ṭabarī’s preferred interpretation, that no one has exclusive privilege over the Sacred Mosque: those settled there and those who come from outside are equal in honouring its sanctity, worshipping therein, circumambulating the House, and performing its rites. The expression has also been understood more broadly as extending to the Sacred Precinct, and some exegetes and jurists further extended this equality to Makkan dwellings (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī). al-Ṭabarī prefers that the aya establishes equality in access to worship and the rites rather than determining ownership of Makkan homes. Other exegetes and jurists, however, derived from it different rulings regarding the ownership, sale, inheritance, and rental of Makkan property. Ibn Taymiyyah, for example, allows sale and inheritance but not rental to pilgrims, while Ibn al-Qayyim adopts a more restrictive view of private ownership in Makkah.
 [4] That is, whoever deliberately intends deviation from uprightness within the Sacred Mosque through wrongdoing. The immediate referent of “therein” is the Sacred Mosque, although many exegetes extend the heightened sanctity and warning to the entire Sacred Precinct (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Shinqīṭī). Ẓulm (“wrongdoing”) is general on al-Ṭabarī’s preferred interpretation and encompasses every act of disobedience, from Association and grave sins to lesser offences, whereas other exegetes give particular applications, including Association, deliberately violating the Sanctuary’s inviolability, unlawful killing or hunting, and other transgressions. Ibn ʿĀshīūr gives special contextual prominence to Association, which drove the Quraysh to oppose the Believers and bar them from the Sanctuary (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). The wording also raises a distinctive question concerning intention. Some scholars understood the aya to mean that, because of the exceptional sanctity of the Sacred Precinct, even a deliberate resolve to commit wrongdoing there may incur punishment before the act is carried out. al-Shinqīṭī also allows that irādah here means firm and settled resolve, which is itself sinful wherever it occurs, unlike a fleeting thought or an intention abandoned for God’s sake. The deliberateness therefore comes from yurid (“intends”), not from bi-ẓulm itself (cf. al-Shinqīṭī). Wrongdoing in the Sacred Precinct is correspondingly graver because of the sanctity of the place, even though its gravity is magnified rather than its numerical count necessarily multiplied (cf. Ibn al-Qayyim).

[1]And [mention, O Muhammad] when We designated[2] for Ibrāhīm (Abraham) the site of the House:[3] “Associate nothing with Me, and purify My House[4] for those who circumambulate, those who stand [in Prayer], and those who bow and prostrate.

[1] After mentioning the Deniers’ barring others from the Sacred Mosque and warning against deviation therein, the passage recalls Abraham (عليه السلام), the forefather of the Makkan Arabs, and the original purpose for which the House was established: the exclusive worship of God and its purification for those who worship there. Whoever deviates within the Sacred Mosque thereby violates the very purpose for which God designated its site to Abraham and commanded him to establish the House there. The recollection also rebukes the Quraysh for abandoning Abraham’s way, polluting the House with idols, and barring the people of Divine Oneness from worshipping there (cf. Abīū Ḥayyān, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). “Associate nothing with Me” places Divine Oneness at the foundation of all that follows: no act of worship is sound without exclusive devotion to God. “Purify My House” includes, foremost, purification from Association and idols, but exegetes extend it more broadly to every religious, moral, and physical defilement that compromises the sanctity of the House or obstructs its worshippers (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī). The majority understand these commands as addressed to Abraham (عليه السلام), although a minority interpretation takes the addressee to be Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ).
 [2] BawwaÒnā means that We prepared and designated the site of the House for Abraham (عليه السلام). The root b-w-Ò is associated with settling in a place and taking it as a dwelling; mabāʾah denotes a place of settlement. Here the expression does not mean that Abraham was given the House as a personal dwelling, but that its location was appointed and made ready for him to establish the House and its worship. Some exegetes further explain that the site or earlier foundations had become concealed and were shown to him (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; al-Ṭabarī).
 [3] God Almighty prepared the site of the Kaʿbah for Abraham (عليه السلام), showed him its location, and established him there, commanding him to build the House upon pure worship: “Associate nothing with Me”, that is, Associate nothing with God in worship and devote all deeds sincerely to Him Alone (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, al-Saʿdī). Ibn Kathīr observes that this constitutes a rebuke to the Quraysh, who worshipped others besides God and Associated partners with Him in the very place established from the outset upon Divine Oneness and the worship of God Alone, with no partner. The ordering is itself significant: the rejection of Association precedes the commands to purify the House and perform its rites, underscoring that Divine Oneness is the foundation upon which worship is established.
 [4] “Purify My House” commands Abraham (عليه السلام) to keep the House free from everything unworthy of its sanctity, foremost Association and Denial, but also religious innovations, sins, indecencies, injustice, physical impurities, and every form of defilement, so that it remains pure for those who circumambulate, stand in worship, bow, and prostrate (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī). al-Saʿdī adds that these worshippers have a special right to honour and consideration, which includes keeping the House free even from idle or raised voices that disturb those engaged in Prayer and circumambulation. The designation “My House” is an attribution of honour, not of indwelling: the House is ascribed to God because of its special consecration and distinction as a place devoted to His worship Alone (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
And proclaim[1] [O Ibrāhīm][2] the Hajj among mankind; they shall come to you on foot[3] and on every lean mount;[4] they shall come from every distant pass,[5]

[1] That is, announce to people, O Abraham, that Hajj to the House of God is obligatory upon them, and call them to come as pilgrims (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, Ibn Kathīr).
 [2] al-Shinqīṭī holds that “And proclaim [O Ibrāhīm] the Hajj among mankind” is addressed to Abraham (عليه السلام), as the context indicates and as held by the majority of scholars.
 [3] Rijālan means “pilgrims travelling on foot”. It is the plural of rājil, one who travels on foot, and is derived from the root r-j-l, associated with the foot (cf. Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; al-Kafawī, al-Kulliyyāt). Some scholars inferred from the mention of walking before riding that performing Hajj on foot is preferable, particularly because it entails greater exertion. The majority, however, hold that riding is preferable, following the practice of The Prophet (ﷺ), who performed Hajj riding despite being physically able to walk (cf. al-Shinqīṭī).
 [4] Ḍāmir (“lean mount”) signals an animal lean in flesh, commonly through the length and exertion of travel. al-Ṭabarī and many exegetes understand it specifically as a lean camel, while Ibn ʿĀshīūr treats ḍāmir more broadly as a mount and notes that such leanness is a desirable quality in riding animals because it aids movement; al-Shinqīṭī likewise explains it as “a camel or the like”. The broader rendering “every lean mount” reflects this wider sense without excluding the predominant camel-specific interpretation. The root ḍ-m-r signifies thinness or leanness in a thing (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn Juzayy, Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān; al-Kafawī, al-Kulliyyāt; Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī). The feminine plural yaÒtīna (“they come”) refers collectively to the many mounts encompassed by kull ḍāmir. al-Ṭabarī takes the intended referent particularly as the she-camels, while Ibn ʿĀshīūr explains that kull gives the expression a collective sense and may here convey abundance, namely numerous mounts rather than literally every individual mount.
 [5] Fajj ʿamīq (“every distant pass”) implies a remote route or mountain pass. The root f-j-j conveys opening and separation, and fajj means a broad road or passage, especially one running between mountains. Ibn ʿĀshīūr notes that the word came to be used more generally for a road because many routes leading to Makkah pass between mountains. ʿAmīq literally denotes depth, but here means distant or remote; Ibn ʿĀshīūr understands this either as a figurative extension of the word or as an image in which Makkah is conceived as elevated and the pilgrims as ascending towards it (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān; Ibn ʿĀshīūr).

that they may witness benefits for themselves[1] and mention the Name of Allah during known days[2] over what He has provided them of livestock animals.[3] So eat thereof and feed the destitute poor. [4]

[1] That is, the pilgrims come to attain the many benefits of Hajj, encompassing benefits in this worldly life and the Hereafter. These include religious benefits such as forgiveness, reward, and other acts pleasing to God, as well as worldly benefits such as lawful trade (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Saʿdī). al-Ṭabarī prefers this comprehensive interpretation because the word manāfiʿ (“benefits”) is left unrestricted. al-Rasʿanī reports: “Ibn ʿAbbās and most exegetes said: it means trade and markets.” Among the benefits of Hajj in the Hereafter are forgiveness of sins and entry into the Garden. Abīū Hurayrah (رضي الله عنه) reported that The Prophet (ﷺ) said: “Whoever performs Hajj to this House and neither engages in obscenity nor commits sin returns like the day his mother gave birth to him” (al-Bukhārī: 1820; Muslim: 1350). He also reported that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: “One ʿUmrah to the next is an expiation for what is between them, and an accepted Hajj has no reward except Paradise” (al-Bukhārī: 1773; Muslim: 1349).
 [2] “Known days” is understood by the majority of exegetes as the first ten days of Dhīū al-Ḥijjah, from the first through the Day of Sacrifice on the tenth. Another substantial interpretation takes them to be the Days of Sacrifice themselves, whether the Day of Sacrifice and the following two days or, according to another view, the following three as well (cf. Ibn Abī Zamanīn, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Bayḍāwī, Ibn Rajab, Laṭāʾif al-Maʿārif; Muqātil Ibn Sulaymān, al-Samarqandī, al-Zajjāj, Maʿānī al-Qur’ān wa-Iʿrābuh; al-Wāḥidī, al-Shawkānī, al-Shinqīṭī). al-Shinqīṭī strongly prefers the latter interpretation. He argues that “mention the Name of Allah during known days over what He has provided them of livestock animals” refers immediately to mentioning Allah’s Name when slaughtering the sacrificial animals. The following command to eat from them further confirms, in his view, that these are the days on which slaughter takes place. He therefore identifies the known days as the Days of Sacrifice, certainly the tenth, eleventh and twelfth of Dhīū al-Ḥijjah, while recording disagreement over whether the thirteenth is also included (cf. al-Shinqīṭī).
