More broadly, the aya also encompasses remembrance of and gratitude to God for His favour in providing grazing livestock, particularly animals used for transport and sacrifice during Hajj (cf. al-Samʿānī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Juzayy, al-Saʿdī). The disagreement over the “known days” also bears directly on the juristic question of how long sacrificial slaughter remains valid. al-Biqāʿī further distinguishes the “known days” here from the “numbered days” of Aya 2: 203. On the majority interpretation, the beginning of Dhīū al-Ḥijjah must first be carefully established so that these days and the rites culminating in the Day of Sacrifice are known, whereas the Days of Tashrīq, once the Day of Sacrifice has been established, need only be counted in sequence. Compare the parallel aya: “Mention Allah in ˹these˺ numbered days” (2: 203).
 [3] Bahīmat al-anʿām (“livestock animals”) refers specifically to camels, cattle, sheep, and goats. Bahīmah symbolises an animal lacking articulate speech or discernible expression, while al-anʿām restricts the reference here to these recognised livestock animals. The root n-ʿ-m, to which anʿām is related, conveys ease, well-being, and wholesome living, reflecting the benefit and provision associated with livestock (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān; Ibn Kathīr).
 [4] al-bāʾis al-faqīr (“the destitute poor”) denotes one afflicted by severe poverty and distress. al-faqīr further describes and intensifies al-bāʾis, while b-Ò-s conveys severity, hardship, and distress. The expression may encompass one afflicted by poverty, hunger, incapacity, or other pressing needs (cf. al-Naḥḥās, Maʿānī al-Qur’ān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Rāzī, Mukhtār al-Ṣiḥāḥ; al-Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Ṭabarī). “So eat thereof and feed the destitute poor” means eat from the slaughtered sacrificial animals and feed from them those afflicted by severe poverty and need. Exegetes and jurists differed over the force of “eat thereof”. The majority understand it as permission or recommendation rather than obligation, partly in contrast to the pre-Islamic practice of refraining from eating sacrificial animals; a minority regarded the command as obligatory. The ruling also differs according to the type of sacrifice (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Shinqīṭī).
Then let them remove their unkemptness,[1] fulfil their vows,[2] and circumambulate[3] the Time-Honoured House.[4]

[1] Thumma l-yaqḍīū tafathahum (“Then let them remove their unkemptness”) has been explained in two closely related ways. Tafath may represent the physical effects of iḥrām and travel, including dishevelment, dirt, overgrown hair and nails, which are removed upon release from iḥrām through such acts as shaving or shortening the hair, trimming the nails and moustache, and cleansing the body. It has also been understood more broadly as completing the remaining rites of Hajj, including stoning the pillars, sacrifice, shaving, and, in some early explanations, ṭawāf (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). The word tafath itself indicates dirt, grime, or the state of bodily dishevelment. Niẓām al-Dīn al-Nīsābīūrī reports exegetical agreement that removing such grime and bodily overgrowth, including trimming the moustache and nails and removing unwanted hair, falls within its meaning. This should not, however, be taken to exclude the broader early interpretation of tafath as encompassing the remaining rites of Hajj. The imperative lām in thumma l-yaqḍīū is recited both with sukīūn, l-yaqḍīū, and with kasrah, li-yaqḍīū, according to the canonical readings; the difference has no effect on the meaning. Ibn ʿĀshīūr further explains that thumma here need not impose a rigid chronological sequence, but may mark progression in discourse and importance.
 [2] “Fulfil their vows” means that the pilgrims should discharge whatever they have undertaken as binding upon themselves in connection with Hajj. Ibn ʿAbbās understood this particularly as slaughtering sacrificial animals they had vowed, while Mujāhid included a vowed Hajj, sacrificial offerings, and anything else vowed in connection with the pilgrimage. Another interpretation takes nudhīūrahum (“their vows”) more broadly to include what has become binding upon them of the rites and obligations of Hajj, since Arabic may describe one who has discharged what is due upon him as having “fulfilled his vow” (cf. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī). By comparison, Ibn ʿĀshīūr understands the expression specifically as referring to more devotional acts undertaken beyond the obligatory rites, such as an additional circumambulation, retreat in the Sacred Mosque, a sacrificial offering, or feeding the poor. The aya also supports the obligation of fulfilling a valid vow of obedience; a vow involving disobedience is not to be fulfilled (cf. al-Qurṭubī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī).
 [3] “Circumambulate the Time-Honoured House” is overwhelmingly understood as referring to Ṭawāf al-Ifāḍah, also called Ṭawāf al-Ziyārah, the obligatory circumambulation of Hajj performed after standing at ʿArafah, either on the Day of Sacrifice or thereafter. al-Ṭabarī states that the exegetes are in agreement on this interpretation, and al-Qurṭubī likewise identifies it as the obligatory Ṭawāf al-Ifāḍah. al-Ṭabarī, nevertheless, transmits an isolated report from Zuhayr interpreting it as the Farewell Ṭawāf, so the claim of unanimity should be understood as reflecting the overwhelmingly predominant interpretation rather than an absolute absence of dissent. The dominant interpretation clearly remains Ṭawāf al-Ifāḍah, which is a pillar of Hajj. The sequence of the clauses does not necessarily impose a strict legal order, since the conjunction “and” does not by itself require chronological succession (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī).
 [4] “The Time-Honoured House” translates al-Bayt al-ʿAtīq and specifically denotes the Kaʿbah. The description ʿatīq has been explained principally in three ways: ancient, because it is the first House established for mankind as a place of worship; freed or protected from tyrants; and noble or excellent. The root ʿ-t-q carries the senses of antiquity and nobility, while freedom or emancipation is also an established meaning (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-Qur’ān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; al-Rāzī, Mukhtār al-Ṣiḥāḥ; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān; al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Shinqīṭī). al-Shinqīṭī holds that the Qur’anic evidence particularly supports antiquity and primacy, citing the description of the Kaʿbah as “The first House ˹of worship˺ laid down for mankind” (3: 96), while accepting the other interpretations as valid. The interpretation that the House is ʿatīq because God freed it from the domination of tyrants is well established in the exegetical tradition and is supported by the report from ʿAbdullāh Ibn al-Zubayr (رضي الله عنهما) that The Prophet (ﷺ) said: “It is called the Time-Honoured House because no tyrant prevailed over it” (al-Tirmidhī: 3170). This is a transmitted exegetical explanation; hadith scholars have differed over the strength of the report, and the statement is not an unqualified claim about every historical attack upon the House. The description “the Time-Honoured House” occurs again in Aya 33. Its repetition may be understood as reinforcing the House’s ancient sanctity and its foundation upon pure worship, particularly against the background of the Quraysh’s Association and their obstruction of worshippers from the Sacred Mosque. In Aya 33, however, “their lawful place of sacrifice is by the Time-Honoured House” does not mean that the sacrificial animals are slaughtered beside the Kaʿbah itself. One interpretation takes “the House” there broadly for the Sacred Precinct, while another understands the rites as culminating in circumambulation of the House. Ibn Taymiyyah further observes that the antiquity of a place of worship is itself praiseworthy: an ancient mosque is further removed from the suspicion of having been newly built for harmful purposes, and its long history ordinarily entails a greater accumulation of worship therein. He explicitly connects this with al-Bayt al-ʿAtīq and with the Kaʿbah being the first House established for mankind (cf. Ibn Taymiyyah, Majmīūʿ al-Fatāwā, 17: 469).

[1]Such [is the command]. [2]And whoever venerates the sanctities[3] of Allah, it is better for him in the regard of his Lord. [4]Grazing livestock have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you [as unlawful].[5] [6]So avoid the filth of idols, and avoid [7]false speech,

[1] Dhālika (literally, “that”) is used here as a concise transition in the discourse. Ibn ʿĀshīūr understands it as separating two sections, or two aspects of the same discourse, while drawing attention to the importance of what follows. Grammatically, he takes it as a subject with an omitted predicate, with an implied sense such as “that is a statement” or “that is a reminder”. The far demonstrative also points to the elevated rank and importance of what has just been mentioned. Other exegetes and grammarians supply such meanings as “the prescribed duty is such” or “observe that”; al-Ṭabarī specifically understands it as referring to the preceding commands as the duties prescribed for the pilgrims. Hence, the rendering “Such [is the command]” makes explicit one recognised interpretation of the Arabic ellipsis (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] “Such [is the command]” refers, on al-Ṭabarī’s interpretation, to what God has just commanded concerning Hajj: “remove their unkemptness, fulfil their vows, and circumambulate the Time-Honoured House” (22: 29). These rites are among the ḥurumāt Allāh, the things God has made sacred and inviolable. To honour them is to fulfil His commands with due reverence and care, while also avoiding any violation of His limits and prohibitions. Whoever thus honours God’s sanctities, “it is better for him in the regard of his Lord”, in his religion, worldly life, and Hereafter (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn al-Qayyim, Madārij al-Sālikīn; Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī).
 [3] The address here turns to the Muslims, reminding them that Islam did not abolish the sanctity of these matters, but preserved them upon their original Abrahamic foundation. Ḥurumāt Allāh (“the sanctities of Allah”) encompasses everything God has commanded to be honoured and not violated, including the rites of Hajj, the Sacred Mosque, the Sacred House, the Sacred Land, the sacred month, the person while in iḥrām, the sacrificial offerings, al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām, and the other sacred rites and limits connected with pilgrimage. To venerate them is to treat each according to the sanctity God has assigned to it, fulfilling what He has commanded and avoiding neglect, desecration, and transgression of His limits (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [4] This invalidates the religious prohibitions that the Associators invented concerning livestock, such as the baḥīrah, sāʾibah, waṣīlah, and al-ḥāmī, as well as certain prohibitions concerning unborn offspring. Such restrictions possessed no Divine authority: the Associators prohibited what God had made lawful and falsely attributed these prohibitions to Him. The principle is that the authority to declare something lawful or unlawful belongs to God Alone; religious prohibitions may not be invented and attributed to Him without Revelation. The exception, “except what is recited to you”, preserves those prohibitions genuinely established by Revelation (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Ṭabarī). “Allah allowed none ˹of the so-called˺ baḥīrah, nor sā’ibah, nor waṣīlah, nor ḥām but the Deniers fabricate lies against Allah; most of them have no sense” (5: 103).
 [5] “Grazing livestock have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you [as unlawful]” means that camels, cattle, sheep, and goats are lawful to eat when lawfully slaughtered, except where Revelation has established a prohibition. Such prohibitions include carrion, flowing blood, animals dedicated to other than God, and animals killed in the prohibited ways detailed elsewhere in the Qur’an. The same revealed lists also prohibit swine flesh, although swine are not themselves included among al-anʿām (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī). The clause is especially appropriate in the context of Hajj because slaughter and sacrifice form part of its rites, so the aya clarifies the general lawfulness of livestock while preserving the prohibitions established by Revelation. al-Qurṭubī also records another interpretation linking the exception with the prohibition of hunting while in iḥrām (cf. al-Qurṭubī). Ibn ʿĀshīūr further notes that the present tense in “what is recited to you” allows the expression to encompass both prohibitions already revealed and continually recited, and those subsequently revealed.
 [6] After urging the veneration of God’s sanctities, the aya commands the avoidance of idols and false speech, for Divine Oneness, the rejection of all partners, and truthfulness in speech are among the greatest of those sanctities. Association itself is a form of falsehood, for the Associator falsely claims that an idol or another created being deserves worship. Consequently, the two prohibitions are brought together, while “avoid” is repeated to give false speech independent emphasis (cf. al-Zamakhsharī, Abīū Ḥayyān). The connection with the preceding declaration that livestock animals have been made lawful is also significant. The Associators had invented religious prohibitions concerning livestock and falsely attributed them to God; idols and fabricated claims about God therefore lay behind those restrictions. Qawl al-zīūr (“false speech”), however, is broader than this immediate context and encompasses lying, false testimony, fabricated religious claims, and every statement that departs from the Truth (cf. al-Biqāʿī, Abīū Ḥayyān).
 [7] Qawl al-zīūr (“false speech”) conveys falsehood, lying, fabrication, and every statement that departs from the Truth. The root z-w-r expresses deviation or turning aside; falsehood is called zīūr because it turns away from the path of Truth (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; al-Kafawī, al-Kulliyyāt). The command “avoid false speech” is much broader than merely refraining from a particular lie. Ijtanibīū calls for keeping away from falsehood and its practices altogether. It includes lying, false testimony, Association, and speaking about God without knowledge. In the immediate context, this particularly exposes the Associators’ fabricated claims concerning livestock, declaring things lawful or unlawful without Divine warrant. Association itself is the gravest falsehood, since it falsely assigns the right of worship to something besides God (cf. Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī). This is closely related to His Words: “Say ˹Muhammad˺: ‘My Lord only forbade vices, both open and secret, sinning, aggressing unrightfully, that you Associate with Him that for which He sent down no authority, and that you say about Allah what you have no knowledge of’” (7: 33). The fabricated livestock prohibitions condemned in Ayas 6: 143–145 provide another clear instance of such speech. Abīū Bakrah (رضي الله عنه) reported that The Prophet (ﷺ) said three times: “Shall I not inform you of the gravest of the major sins?” They said: “Yes, Messenger of Allah.” He said: “Associating partners with Allah and undutifulness to parents.” He had been reclining, then sat up and said: “And indeed, false speech!” He continued repeating it until they wished he would stop (al-Bukhārī: 2654; Muslim: 87). Abīū Hurayrah (رضي الله عنه) reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: “Whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, Allah has no need of his giving up his food and drink” (al-Bukhārī: 1903). This is a severe warning against allowing falsehood to undermine the moral purpose and reward of fasting; it does not mean that such speech by itself formally invalidates the fast.

[being rightly] inclining wholly to Allah, not Associating anything with Him.[1] Whoever Associates anything with Allah, it is as though he had fallen from the sky, whereupon birds snatch him away,[2] or the wind hurls him down into a far-off place.[3]

[1] Ḥunafāʾa lillāh (“inclining wholly to Allah”) describes those who are upright upon pure Divine Oneness, turning away from falsehood towards Truth and devoting their worship and obedience exclusively to God. Grammatically, ḥunafāʾa is a circumstantial expression (ḥāl) describing the state in which the command to “avoid the filth of idols, and avoid false speech” is to be fulfilled: they are to keep away from these things while wholly devoted to God (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). The following expression, ghayra mushrikīna bihi (“not Associating anything with Him”), further explains this state. The two expressions combine affirmation and negation: ḥunafāʾa lillāh affirms exclusive devotion to God, while ghayra mushrikīna bihi excludes every form of Association (cf. Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] This parable portrays the utter ruin of Association. The one who Associates partners with God is likened to a person falling from the sky, then either being snatched and torn apart by birds or swept away by the wind to a far-off place. al-Ṭabarī understands the image broadly as depicting destruction and extreme distance from guidance and Truth. al-Shawkānī and al-Saʿdī further explain the sky as representing the elevation and protection of Faith, while the fall represents descent into the degradation of Association. The two possible outcomes, being torn apart by birds or carried away by the wind to a distant place, both convey helplessness, irretrievable loss, and the absence of any means of rescue (cf. Muqātil Ibn Sulaymān, al-Ṭabarī, al-Shawkānī, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī). al-Shinqīṭī adds an important qualification: this inescapable ruin applies to one who dies upon Association without repentance. Whoever sincerely repents before death may be forgiven.
 [3] The second image completes the portrayal of ruin: alternatively, the wind seizes him and hurls him into an exceedingly remote place from which there is no escape. Saḥīq denotes something exceedingly distant or remote. The two images, being snatched away by birds or being swept by the wind into a far-off place, both portray the utter ruin and remoteness from the Truth brought about by Association. al-Ṭabarī understands the parable generally as depicting destruction and extreme distance from guidance, while al-Shawkānī and al-Saʿdī further relate the fall from the sky to descent from the elevation of Faith into Association. Ibn ʿĀshīūr also understands the two alternatives as alluding to two kinds of Associators: one whose Association is wavering and unstable, and another firmly settled in it. He adds that deliverance through repentance remains possible so long as a person has not died upon Association, albeit for some it may be exceedingly remote (cf. Muqātil Ibn Sulaymān, al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Samʿānī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī).
[1]Such [is the command]. And whoever venerates the Symbols[2] of Allah, that is indeed from the Mindfulness of hearts.[3]

[1] “Such [is the command]” refers back to the preceding injunctions to avoid idolatry and false speech, to be observed in wholehearted devotion to God without Association. The phrase ḥunafāʾa lillāhi ghayra mushrikīna bihi is circumstantial, describing the state of those fulfilling these commands (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī). Grammatically, dhālika admits three analyses: a subject with an omitted predicate, “That is Allah’s command”; the predicate of an omitted subject, “[The command is] that”; or the object of an omitted verb, “[Follow] that” (cf. al-Qurṭubī). God’s Symbols are understood as the manifest ordinances of religion generally, the places and rites of Hajj specifically, or the sacrificial animals in particular (cf. al-Qurṭubī). al-Ṭabarī favours a meaning encompassing the places and acts prescribed for Hajj (cf. al-Ṭabarī). The ensuing discussion of sacrifice supports this contextual emphasis, with sacrificial animals expressly included among God’s Symbols in Aya 36. Ibn ʿĀshīūr regards the Symbols here as more specific than the Sanctities mentioned in Aya 30, explaining that their particular mention after the broader category draws attention to their importance (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] “Symbols of Allah”: shaʿāÒir, the plural of shaʿīrah, highlights what God has appointed as visible markers of obedience to Him. The relevant sense of the root sh-ʿ-r is knowledge, perception or awareness, from which comes the sense of a distinguishing marker through which something becomes known and recognisable (cf. al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān).
 [3] Whoever “venerates the Symbols of Allah” honours the outward markers that God has appointed for His worship, which here pertain particularly to the Hajj rites and sacrificial animals. Such veneration includes performing the rites as God commands and honouring the sacrificial animals by selecting fine specimens, fattening them, and offering them in the best condition (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr). It springs from the Mindfulness of hearts and bears witness to sound Faith, for honouring what God has appointed for His worship follows from honouring and revering God Himself (cf. al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
In them[1] there are benefits[2] for you until an appointed term; then their lawful place of sacrifice is by the Time-Honoured House.[3]

[1] This most directly refers to the sacrificial animals. Exegetes differ over the period during which their benefits may be enjoyed: some understand it as ending when the animals are designated as offerings; others permit certain benefits until slaughter, subject to conditions. On the latter view, the animals may be ridden when needed, without harming them, and milk may be taken after their offspring have received enough. Any removal of wool or hair must neither harm nor diminish the animals. The majority interpretation takes the pronoun as referring to sacrificial animals, and al-Rāzī considers this the closer reading in light of the following words, “then their lawful place of sacrifice is by the Time-Honoured House.” Here, “the House” encompasses the Sacred Precinct, including Minā, rather than only the immediate vicinity of the Kaʿbah. Other exegetes understand “them” more broadly as referring to the Symbols of God generally. On this reading, the benefits vary according to each Symbol, including benefits derived from sacrificial animals, worship and trade at the sacred sites, and the religious and worldly benefits of the Hajj rites and appointed periods. The “appointed term” likewise varies with the referent, such as the completion of the Hajj days or departure from the sacred sites (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr, Abīū al-Suʿīūd, al-Shawkānī, al-Saʿdī).
 [2] This aya permits benefit from sacrificial offerings destined for the Sacred Precinct (hady) until slaughter, provided that such use neither harms nor unduly weakens them. This includes riding them or carrying loads upon them when needed, and drinking surplus milk after their offspring have received enough. Jurists differ over the extent of permissible benefit after designation as an offering, particularly whether need is a condition. Ibn ʿĀshīūr explains that the aya also refutes the practice of the Associators, who forbade themselves such benefits once an offering had been garlanded or marked: venerating an offering does not require renouncing every lawful benefit from it (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [3] “Their lawful place of sacrifice” translates maḥilluhā, here the appointed destination where the sacrificial animals may lawfully be slaughtered. The term can also denote the appointed time of slaughter. The root ḥ-l-l conveys untying, release, and becoming lawful; it also carries the sense of arriving and settling at a place (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn ʿĀshīūr). “Then their lawful place of sacrifice is by the Time-Honoured House” means that the offerings reach their appointed destination within the Sacred Precinct, where they are slaughtered in accordance with the conditions prescribed for them. “The House” here encompasses the Sacred Precinct, including Minā; it does not designate the Kaʿbah or the Mosque itself as the place of slaughter. The House is named because it is the goal of Hajj and the noblest part of the Sacred Precinct, as in “as a gifted offering reaching the Kaʿbah” (5: 95) (cf. al-Wāḥidī, al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī). In another interpretation, which takes the pronoun as referring more broadly to the Hajj rites, these culminate in Ṭawāf al-Ifāḍah at the House, in connection with completing the release from iḥrām (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī). Compare the use of maḥill for sacrificial offerings in 2: 196, while noting that offerings made by those prevented from completing the pilgrimage are subject to distinct rulings concerning their place of slaughter.

[1]And for every community[2] We appointed a sacrificial rite,[3] that they may mention the Name of Allah over what He has provided them of grazing livestock. Your God is One God; so, to Him submit.[4] And give glad tidings to the humbly devout;[5]

[1] This passage may be read as preparing the Believers to uphold the Abrahamic character of the House and its rites: worship devoted to God Alone, purified from Association, idolatrous sacrifice, false restrictions on livestock, and obstruction of access to the Sacred Mosque. This is a thematic connection, rather than a statement that responsibility for the House had already passed to them. The declaration “And for every community We appointed a sacrificial rite” (22: 34) follows the purification of the House, the proclamation of Hajj, and the veneration of God’s Symbols. In this context, the rite particularly concerns sacrifice performed with God’s Name mentioned over the animals (cf. al-Ṭabarī). As Ibn ʿĀshīūr observes, the sura rebukes the Associators for claiming allegiance to Abraham and his House while contradicting his devotion to God Alone. The command to give glad tidings to “the humbly devout” (22: 34) connects these observances with the disposition required of those who perform them. Their humility accords with the sura’s repeated call to prostration and surrender before Divine Majesty. They are described through four characteristics: their hearts tremble when God is mentioned, they patiently endure what befalls them, they establish Prayer, and they spend from what He provides (22: 35). Inward reverence thus finds expression in steadfastness, worship, and generosity. The glad tidings recur in “And give glad tidings to the Doers of Excellence” (22: 37), following the declaration that neither the flesh nor the blood of sacrificial animals reaches God, but their offerors’ Mindfulness reaches Him. The outward rite, including feeding others, is thereby joined to its inward purpose. Proper observance requires sincerity and reverence; the physical act alone does not fulfil that purpose. The passage then moves from worship to Divine protection: “Verily Allah ever defends those who Believe” (22: 38). Permission to fight follows for those who have suffered injustice and expulsion from their homes (22: 39–40). Ibn ʿĀshīūr understands this permission as an expression of the defence just promised. The mention of monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques threatened with destruction widens the concern to the protection of worship alongside the defence of the wronged. Those granted establishment in the land are so described as people who “keep up the Prayer, give zakat [willingly], enjoin virtue, and advise against what is unacceptable” (22: 41). These are the religious and communal responsibilities that faithful empowerment should produce. The reference to an appointed rite returns in 22: 67, where mansak is variously understood as a festival, sacrifice, or prescribed religious way. Although its scope need not be identical to that in 22: 34, the recurrence reinforces the connection between appointed observances and devotion to God. Near the sura’s close, “Bow and prostrate, worship your Lord, and do good” (22: 77) brings humility, worship, and righteous action together. “Strive in the cause of Allah with the striving due to Him” (22: 78) then connects the Believers’ calling with Divine choice, freedom from hardship in religion, and the way of their father Abraham. Hajj accordingly forms a thematic centre through which the sura brings together Abrahamic devotion, Mindfulness, humility, generosity, and the protection of worship. The responsibility suggested by this sequence is to serve God’s House, uphold its rites, and preserve access to it for worship.
 [2] “Community” translates ummah: here, a people united by adherence to the same religion (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [3] “A sacrificial rite” translates mansak: here, the slaughter of offerings as an act of worship and a means of drawing near to God. The word may more broadly suggest a religious rite, its place, or its appointed time. Its root, n-s-k, demonstrates worship and drawing near to God; the mention of livestock makes sacrificial slaughter the strongest contextual interpretation here (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Wāḥidī, al-Basīṭ and al-Wajīz; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb). Every former community of Believers was prescribed sacrificial worship, though its particular forms and regulations could differ. They were to “mention the Name of Allah” Alone over the camels, cattle, sheep, and goats He provided, dedicating their sacrifice exclusively to Him and seeking His Countenance and Pleasure. “Over” may indicate mentioning God’s Name when slaughtering the animals, or carry the sense of remembering and thanking Him for providing them. The rite therefore unites remembrance and gratitude with exclusive devotion to God, as the following declaration of Divine Oneness and command to submit to Him make clear (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Basīṭ; al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, Naẓm al-Durar; al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [4] “Your God is One God; so, to Him submit” connects the sacrificial worship appointed for successive communities with Divine Oneness. Ibn ʿĀshīūr explains that the shared institution of sacrifice points to the Oneness of God, Who appointed it; exclusive submission follows from that Oneness. Placing “to Him” first emphasises this exclusivity: submit to Him Alone. The command calls for sincere inward and outward obedience, abandoning rites devoted to others and observing sacrifice as God prescribes. Much as revealed laws and ritual forms may differ among communities, the call to worship God Alone remains unchanged (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr): “We have not sent any Messenger before you ˹Muhammad˺ but We reveal to him that: ‘There is no God but Me, so worship Me ˹Alone˺!’” (21: 25). A spiritual implication of this submission is readiness to obey, even when the full wisdom of a prescribed rite is not apparent, as with certain observances of Hajj. Within the sura’s wider movement, the command may also be read as preparing the Believers for the responsibilities that follow. Humble devotion and patience are described immediately afterwards (22: 35), followed by Divine defence, permission to fight for those wronged, and the duties accompanying establishment in the land (22: 38–41). The sura later culminates in the call to strive in God’s cause (22: 78). Complete submission to God Alone provides the spiritual foundation for these responsibilities.
 [5] “The humbly devout” translates al-mukhbitīn: those who humbly submit to God, with sincere, tranquil hearts and reverent obedience. The term encompasses humility, trust in God, repentance, and submission in heart and deed (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn al-Qayyim). Ibn ʿĀshīūr explains its imagery through khabt, low-lying ground: mukhbit originally describes someone travelling through such ground, then metaphorically someone who follows the path of humility. Here it describes the Believers, whose humility contrasts with the arrogance of the Associators: “Thus does Allah seal every heart of an arrogant tyrant” (40: 35). This description is particularly fitting in the context of Hajj, whose rites embody surrender and humility. Abīū Ḥayyān draws attention to leaving ordinary habits, traversing dusty and stony places, and undertaking demanding observances. For male pilgrims, setting aside ordinary clothing for the garments of iḥrām and leaving the head uncovered further express this surrender. Such observances cultivate obedience even when their full wisdom is not apparent. The following aya identifies four manifestations of humble devotion: hearts that tremble when God is mentioned, patience in the face of hardship, establishment of Prayer, and spending from His provision. These qualities find expression during Hajj in maintaining Prayer at the pilgrimage sites and giving generously, including through sacrificial offerings, while their application extends beyond the pilgrimage. Spending is required according to one’s means; those who possess nothing to give are not excluded from the humbly devout (cf. Abīū Ḥayyān, Ibn al-Qayyim, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
[1]those whose hearts tremble[2] when Allah is mentioned, who remain patient through whatever befalls them,[3] who establish Prayer,[4] and who spend out of what We have provided them.[5]

[1] The humbly devout are then described by four traits: hearts that tremble when God is mentioned, patience in the face of hardship, including harm suffered in His cause, establishment of Prayer, and spending from what God has provided. All four are manifestations of humility before God (cf. al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). These four traits reveal humility in its inward and outward forms. When God is mentioned, their hearts tremble, because the humble heart responds with reverent fear when reminded of God; it recognises Majesty, feels its own need, and stands inwardly before God as a servant, not as a self-sufficient being. Their patience over what befalls them is another form of humility, for patience restrains sinful objection to God’s decree while allowing natural grief, supplication, and lawful efforts to obtain relief or justice. Their establishment of Prayer embodies humility in disciplined action: the servant observes its prescribed times, conditions, and obligations, joining outward observance with sincerity and humble attentiveness. Their spending from what God has provided shows humility toward wealth and provision, for the giver acknowledges that his genuine ownership depends upon God’s provision and entails duties of obedience and generosity. This indicates that the four traits together describe a servant humbled in heart, humbled under trial, humbled in worship, and humbled in relation to worldly possessions.
 [2] “Whose hearts tremble” translates wajilat qulīūbuhum: their hearts are moved by reverent fear when God is mentioned. Lexically, wajal denotes the inward apprehension of fear. Ibn al-Qayyim describes the Believers’ fear as joined with awe and love (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Qayyim, Shifāʾ al-ʿAlīl; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān; al-Kafawī, al-Kulliyyāt). This is a mark of the true Believers: “Indeed the ˹true˺ Believers are the ones who when Allah is mentioned their hearts tremble with awe, when His Signs are recited for them their Faith increases and they ˹devoutly˺ put their trust in their Lord” (8: 2). It is also the response of those who receive the Qur’an with awe and softness of heart: “Allah has sent down the most beautiful of all teachings: a Book that is consistent and oft-repeated; that causes the skins of those in awe of their Lord to shiver. Then their skins and their hearts soften at the mention of Allah: such is Allah’s Guidance. He guides with it whoever He Wills; no one can guide those Allah leaves to stray” (39: 23).
 [3] Such patience is praised elsewhere: “We shall test you with some fear, hunger and dwindling financial resources, souls and crops—deliver good tidings to those who are patient. *Those who when struck by a calamity say: ‘Verily to Allah we belong and to Him we shall return’. *On those are Prayers from their Lord and Mercy—those are the truly guided” (2: 155-157).
 [4] “Who establish Prayer” means that they perform the prescribed Prayer fully and properly, observing its prescribed times, conditions, and obligations, together with its inward devotion and recommended acts (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Saʿdī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Basīṭ).
 [5] This means that they spend from what God has provided in obligatory and recommended avenues of good: zakat, expiations, maintenance of dependants and relatives entitled to support, voluntary charity to the poor and needy, and spending in God’s cause (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Shawkānī, al-Saʿdī). The particle min in “out of what We have provided them” indicates that they spend a portion of their provision; it does not require them to give everything away. Attributing provision to God reminds them that their ability to acquire wealth depends upon His bounty and facilitation, encouraging gratitude and generosity (cf. al-Saʿdī).

[1]And the [sacrificial] camels ˹and cattle˺,[2] We made them for you among the Symbols of Allah;[3] in them there is good for you.[4] So mention the Name of Allah over them[5] as they stand in rows.[6] Then, when they fall [lifeless] upon their sides,[7] eat thereof and feed the [8] petitioner and [9]the reticent needy.[10] So have We subjected them to you, that you may give thanks [to Me].[11]

[1] After mentioning the prescribed sacrifice through grazing livestock generally, the aya gives particular prominence to camels because of their great size and high standing in people’s estimation. Their being made manageable for human use is itself a manifest Divine favour: although physically larger and stronger than human beings, they yield to human direction because God has made them do so. He could instead have made them wild and unmanageable. Recognising this favour should inspire gratitude, expressed through worshipping Him Alone and observing His commands concerning these animals (cf. al-Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] “[Sacrificial] camels ˹and cattle˺” translates al-budn, the plural of badanah. Exegetes differ over its scope: al-Qurṭubī’s preferred interpretation and Ibn ʿĀshīūr restrict it to sacrificial camels, whereas Ibn ʿAṭiyyah also records its use for camels or cattle designated for sacrifice. The explanatory addition “˹and cattle˺” in the translation acknowledges the inclusive interpretation. al-Qurṭubī supports the narrower meaning with the Prophetic report concerning attendance at Friday Prayer, which distinguishes offering a badanah from offering a cow. Camels and cattle, nevertheless, share certain sacrificial rulings, including the permissibility of seven people sharing an offering. The term derives from badānah, bodily largeness or stoutness, rather than strength as such (cf. al-Qurṭubī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Bukhārī: 881; Muslim: 850, 1318).
 [3] These sacrificial camels and cattle have been made visible emblems of God’s religion. Their prescribed dedication and sacrifice are acts of worship through which nearness to Him is sought. The observances associated with these offerings include bringing them to the Sacred Precinct, garlanding them, marking the sacrificial camels, honouring the animals, mentioning God’s Name when sacrificing them, and feeding others with their meat (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī).
 [4] The sacrificial animals bring worldly benefits, while their offering in obedience to God earns reward in the Hereafter (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī). Mālik Ibn Anas relates that Saʿīd Ibn al-Musayyib performed Hajj accompanied by Ibn Ḥarmalah. Saʿīd bought a ram for sacrifice, while Ibn Ḥarmalah bought a sacrificial camel for six dinars and slaughtered it. When Saʿīd asked why he had not followed his example, Ibn Ḥarmalah replied that he had heard Allah say: “And the [sacrificial] camels ˹and cattle˺, We made them for you among the Symbols of Allah; in them there is good for you” (22: 36), and wished to seek the good wherever Allah had directed him to it. Saʿīd admired his response and thereafter related it from him (cf. Ibn Abī Ḥātim).
 [5] That is, mention God’s Name when sacrificing the camels as they stand arrayed. In the recommended sacrificial posture, a camel’s left foreleg is tethered and it stands on the other three legs. This posture follows the Sunnah; it is not a condition for the validity of the sacrifice (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī).
 [6] “As they stand in rows” translates ṣawāff: standing arrayed at the time of sacrifice. The expression may describe camels arranged beside one another or the ordered posture of an individual camel. The word derives from ṣaff, the arranging of bodies side by side in an ordered line; its root, ṣ-f-f, conveys evenness, alignment, and equality of position (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-QurÒān; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Wāḥidī, al-Basīṭ; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; al-Kafawī, al-Kulliyyāt).
 [7] “Fall [lifeless] upon their sides” is taken to mean wajabat junīūbuhā: when the camels collapse to the ground after sacrifice and their sides come to rest upon it, with life having departed. Skinning or cutting the animal must await its death. Ibn Fāris relates the root w-j-b to falling and occurrence; al-Iṣfahānī also discusses fixity and establishment. Here the intended sense is falling lifeless (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-QurÒān; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān).
 [8] “The petitioner” is rendered as al-qāniʿ: the person who asks humbly for assistance, here for a share of the sacrificial meat. The word has also been related to qanāʿah, contentment with little, and accordingly interpreted as one who remains content and does not ask; the interpretation adopted here, however, contrasts the petitioner with “the reticent needy”, who approaches in hope of receiving without explicitly asking (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-QurÒān; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; al-Azharī, Tahdhīb al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān).
 [9] “The reticent needy” is understood as al-muʿtarr: on the interpretation adopted here, the needy person who approaches in hope of receiving without making an explicit request. The term may also denote one who approaches seeking another’s generosity, whether he asks or remains silent (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-QurÒān; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; al-Fayyīūmī, al-Miṣbāḥ al-Munīr).
 [10] On the interpretation adopted here, al-qāniʿ is the poor person who asks humbly, while al-muʿtarr is one who comes in hope of receiving but refrains from making an explicit request. Other exegetes reverse the two meanings, taking al-qāniʿ as the self-restrained poor person who does not ask and al-muʿtarr as the one who asks. These are two principal interpretations among several transmitted views. Both support feeding the needy from the sacrificial meat, whether their need is voiced openly or discerned from their presence or circumstances (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Samʿānī, al-Māwardī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī). An ethical implication of this Divine Command is that it cultivates moral attentiveness in the giver: compassion for the one whose need compels him to ask, and sensitivity toward the one whose self-restraint keeps him silent. By naming both “the petitioner” and “the reticent needy”, on the interpretation adopted here, the aya trains the Believer to respond, not only to spoken need, but also to concealed hardship. The one who asks must not be despised for the vulnerability of having to ask, while the one who remains silent must not be overlooked merely because he preserves his dignity. True generosity therefore requires more than waiting for a request; it requires attentiveness, discernment, and mercy. The giver learns to recognise need without exposing the needy, to give without wounding, and to preserve the honour of both those who ask and those who refrain from asking (cf. 2: 262–263, 271, 273; 93: 10).
 [11] God’s making livestock manageable for human beings is itself a Divine favour calling for gratitude: “Have they not seen that We created for them, from what Our Hands have made, livestock which they possess? *And We subjected them to them; some of them are their mounts, and from some they eat. *And for them in them are benefits and drinks. Will they not then give thanks [to Me]?” (36: 71-73).

Neither their flesh nor their blood shall ever reach Allah,[1] but what reaches Him is your Mindfulness.[2] Thus has He subjected them to you,[3] that you may Proclaim the Greatness of Allah for having guided you.[4] And give glad tidings to the Doers of Excellence.[5]

[1] This repudiates the practices of the Associators, who sprinkled sacrificial blood at their places of sacrifice and around the Kaʿbah, practised ritual smearing with blood, and displayed portions of sacrificial meat around the House as an offering, in addition to what they distributed to the needy. The aya declares that God has no need of flesh or blood, and that flesh and blood in themselves do not secure His acceptance. Mindfulness joins sincere intention with proper observance, mentioning His Name, and feeding the needy (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] What God accepts and rewards is your Mindfulness (taqwā), sincerity, and obedience in offering the sacrifice solely for Him. The rite is accepted when it is performed seeking His Countenance and pleasure, without pride, ostentation, desire for reputation, or mere adherence to custom, while honouring His sanctities and observing His Commands. Acceptance thereby depends upon sincere devotion joined with observance of the prescribed rite (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Wajīz; Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī). This meaning is reinforced elsewhere in Revelation: “To Him ascends good speech, and righteous deeds He raises” (35: 10). Abīū Hurayrah (رضي الله عنه) relates that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: “Allah does not look at your forms or your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds” (Muslim: 2564). The aya and ḥadīth show that the worth of sacrifice depends upon sincerity, Mindfulness, and righteous performance together.
 [3] “Thus has He subjected them to you, that you may Proclaim the Greatness of Allah” repeats the preceding statement, “So have We subjected them to you,” in order to show that praising God and proclaiming His Greatness for subjecting these animals is a foremost expression of the gratitude enjoined in the previous aya. The two statements thus reinforce one another: gratitude finds a foremost expression in recognising God’s favour, praising Him for it, and proclaiming His Greatness for guiding people to His religion and prescribed rites (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [4] God Almighty made the sacrificial animals manageable so that people might recognise His Greatness and His unique Power to subdue what no one could subdue without His enabling. They are therefore to proclaim His Greatness, affirming His Oneness and Power in gratitude to Him for guiding them to His religion and to the proper sacrificial rites of Hajj (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, al-Saʿdī).
 [5] Excellence does not consist merely in slaughtering the animal, for neither its flesh nor its blood reaches God; rather, it lies in performing the rite with sincere Mindfulness, mentioning God’s Name, feeding both the petitioner and the reticent needy, giving thanks for His favours, and proclaiming His Greatness for His guidance. The Doers of Excellence are hence those who perfect both the outward act of worship and the inward devotion that gives it worth. The glad tidings first given to “the humbly devout” are renewed here for those whose humility is embodied in excellent worship and merciful conduct. The two descriptions may refer to the same Believers, without implying formally successive spiritual ranks (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
[1]Verily Allah ever defends[2] those who Believe; verily Allah does not love anyone who is [3]persistently treacherous and utterly ungrateful.

[1] Having described a number of the rites of Hajj, the discourse turns to the persecution of the Believers and God’s promise to defend them. Abīū Ḥayyān relates the passage to the obstruction at al-Ḥudaybiyah and the eventual return to Makkah. This thematic connection should be distinguished from the commonly reported chronology of Aya 39, the first permission to fight, which followed the migration to Madinah and preceded al-Ḥudaybiyah. The passage promises Divine defence and victory, and describes the responsibilities of those granted establishment in the land (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Abīū Ḥayyān). This passage may be read as continuing the thematic movement already indicated in the introduction and preceding ayas. The rites of Hajj are presented as part of a wider movement from the purification of worship to the defence and eventual empowerment of those who uphold it. Divine support is therefore tied to a clear moral purpose: protecting worship, preserving places in which God’s Name is mentioned, keeping up Prayer, giving zakat, enjoining virtue, and advising against what is unacceptable.
 [2] “Ever defends” translates yudāfiʿu. The Form III pattern often expresses reciprocal action, but here it may carry the sense of the simple form yadfaʿu, “He defends” or “repels”. The simple form is itself a canonical reading. The Form III reading may also convey repeated defence; together with the imperfect tense and the context, this supports “ever defends” (cf. al-Azharī, Maʿānī al-Qirāʾāt; Ibn Zanjalah, Ḥujjat al-Qirāʾāt; Makkī, al-Kashf; al-Wāḥidī, al-Basīṭ; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr). This means that God protects His Believing servants from the harm and schemes of the Deniers and Associators, preserving, delivering, and granting them victory (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī). The promise also bears a wider meaning: by virtue of their Belief, God safeguards them from every form of evil, including the whisperings of Satan, the corruption of their own souls, and the evils arising from their own deeds, and lightens the hardships that would otherwise overwhelm them (cf. al-Saʿdī). This defence is according to their Faith and Divine Wisdom; it does not exempt them from trials or temporary suffering. In one rhetorical explanation, the Form III verb evokes the confrontation between the Deniers’ determined efforts to persecute the Believers and God’s powerful protection of them. Although He is fully Able to destroy their enemies outright, the expression portrays His defence against an aggressively hostile force exerting all its strength to cause them harm (cf. al-Shinqīṭī).
 [3] “Persistently treacherous and utterly ungrateful” renders khawwān kafīūr, two intensive forms. Khawwān denotes one deeply given to betrayal, for Denial violates the covenant by which God called His creatures to worship Him Alone, implanted its recognition within their innate nature, and reaffirmed it through His Messengers. Kafīūr signifies one deeply entrenched in Denial and extreme ingratitude for God’s favours (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr). Such people withhold God’s Rights, violate His Commands and prohibitions, betray the rights of His servants, and break their covenants. Their ingratitude appears in their denial of His favours and refusal to give thanks for them (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī). In the immediate context, the Makkan Associators, particularly the Quraysh, had betrayed the trust associated with their custodianship of the Sacred House by introducing idolatrous practices into the rites of Hajj and barring the Believers from worshipping there. Their ingratitude appears in their corruption of God’s rites, denial of His favours, and refusal to give thanks for them.
Permission [to fight] is granted to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged;[1] Allah is indeed fully Able to grant them victory,[2]

[1] God permits the Believers to fight those who wage war against them, because they have been persecuted for their Faith, subjected to harm, and driven from their homes (cf. al-Wāḥidī, al-Wasīṭ; al-Biqāʿī, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī).
 [2] As discussed under “ever defends” (22: 38), one explanation of the Form III verb evokes the confrontation between the Deniers’ determined efforts to persecute the Believers and God’s powerful protection of them. While He is fully Able to destroy their enemies outright, He legislates the Believers’ armed response as a trial through which people are tested by means of one another: “Such [is the command]. Had Allah Willed, He would have exacted retribution from them, but [He ordained otherwise] to test some of you by means of others” (47: 4) (cf. al-Shinqīṭī).

[1] [they are] those who were driven from their homes without right, merely for saying: “Our Lord is Allah.” [2]Had Allah not repelled some people by means of others,[3] hermitages,[4] fanes,[5] houses of Prayer,[6] and mosques, in which Allah’s Name is abundantly mentioned, would surely have been demolished. Allah will surely grant victory to whoever supports Him; verily Allah is All-Powerful, All-Prevailing.[7]

[1] Having stated that the Believers are permitted to fight because they have been wronged, God identifies two aspects of that injustice: they were “driven from their homes without right”, and they were expelled merely because they declared: “Our Lord is Allah” (cf. al-Rāzī). The same reason for their expulsion is stated elsewhere: “They drive out the Messenger and yourselves because you Believe in Allah, your Lord” (60: 1). According to al-Saʿdī, this passage indicates the wisdom underlying jihād: upholding God’s religion, repelling aggressors who harm the Believers, checking injustice, and enabling worship and the observance of religious rites.
 [2] “Had Allah not repelled some people by means of others” explains the wisdom behind permitting the Believers to fight: were God not to restrain the Associators through those who defend Tawḥīd, they would overpower its followers and destroy their places of worship. God thus legislated fighting for the Muslim community, as He had permitted earlier monotheistic communities to defend themselves, so that aggression would not eradicate worship and the proclamation of His Name. al-Qurṭubī relates the “hermitages, fanes, houses of Prayer” to the earlier revealed communities while their dispensations remained unaltered and operative. Ibn ʿĀshīūr understands the protection more broadly, as benefiting Jewish and Christian places of worship as well as Muslim mosques. These interpretations should therefore be distinguished. Consequently, the aya presents armed defence as a means by which God preserves true religion and protects places dedicated to His worship from destruction. al-Ṭabarī also includes other means of restraining oppression, such as just authority and testimony safeguarding people’s rights (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [3] “Had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, the land would have gone to ruins. But Allah is Favourable to all beings” (2: 251).
 [4] “Hermitages” renders ṣawāmiʿ, the plural of ṣawmaʿah, denoting elevated retreats in which monks and ascetics secluded themselves for worship. Such structures were often narrow or tapering at the top, in keeping with the root sense of slenderness and contraction (cf. al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-ʿAskarī, al-Talkhīṣ fī Maʿrifat Asmāʾ al-Ashyāʾ; al-Wāḥidī, al-Basīṭ; al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān; al-Fayrīūzābādī, Baṣāʾir Dhawī al-Tamyīz).
 [5] “Fanes” renders biyaʿ, the plural of bīʿah, ordinarily denoting Christian places of worship. The word is probably borrowed from Syriac ܒܝܥܬܐ (bēʿṯā), which Jeffery connects with “egg”, the crown of a rounded arch, and hence a domed building used for worship. This proposed etymology does not imply that every building designated by the Arabic term was domed. Its attestation in pre-Islamic South Arabia supports its use in Arabian Christian contexts. The older attribution to Persian is less probable (cf. al-Khalīl, al-ʿAyn; al-Wāḥidī, al-Basīṭ; al-Jawālīqī, al-Muʿarrab; Ibn ʿĀshīūr, Fraenkel, Die aramäischen Fremdwörter im Arabischen; Jeffery, The Foreign Vocabulary of the QurÒān).
 [6] “Houses of Prayer” renders ṣalawāt, interpreted here as Jewish places of worship. One explanation treats the term as an Arabised Aramaic-Syriac designation for a place of prayer, related to ṣlōṯā, “prayer”. Another takes it as the Arabic plural “prayers”, with the act standing for its location or an implied noun yielding “places of prayer” (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-QurÒān; al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Basīṭ; al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt; al-Qurṭubī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; al-Zabīdī, Tāj al-ʿArīūs; Jeffery, The Foreign Vocabulary of the QurÒān). In the exegetical distribution adopted here, the distinctive terms ṣawāmiʿ, biyaʿ, and ṣalawāt evoke historically recognisable forms of worship within the religious landscape known to the Qur’an’s first audience, rather than merely supplying three interchangeable names for places of worship. Ṣawāmiʿ stands for the elevated or secluded retreats of monks and ascetics. Ibn ʿĀshīūr describes a ṣawmaʿah as a tall structure reached by stairs, with a chamber at its summit, in which a monk could withdraw from the distractions of people. Specialised historical research further indicates that, in early Islamic Arabic sources from Syria and Mesopotamia, the term could denote the retreat of a pillar-dwelling ascetic atop a tower or column. Biyaʿ designates communal Christian places of worship and was already established in pre-Islamic Arabian usage, probably as a Syriac loanword. Ṣalawāt here indicates Jewish houses of prayer, as explained above. The renderings “hermitages”, “fanes”, and “houses of Prayer” seek to preserve something of this historical markedness rather than flattening the terms into wholly modern institutional labels. On this interpretation, the sequence moves from the solitary ascetic retreat to Christian communal worship, then to Jewish houses of prayer, and finally to mosques. It presents Divine defence as preserving the institutions of revealed worship from destruction by idolatrous aggression. al-Qurṭubī understands the sanctuaries of the earlier communities in relation to their revealed religions before their subsequent alteration and abrogation by Islam. al-Ṭabarī’s preferred interpretation identifies the four categories as the retreats of monks, Christian places of worship, Jewish houses of worship, and Muslim mosques. Ibn ʿĀshīūr further explains that ṣawāmiʿ are mentioned first because they were especially numerous and familiar in Arabia: travellers recognised their lights, used them for guidance, and sought refuge with their occupants. Biyaʿ follow because they likewise belong to Christian worship, after which come the Jewish ṣalawāt, while masājid occupy the climactic final position as the more general designation. The order is therefore culturally and rhetorically significant, portraying the breadth of religious life preserved through Divine defence (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, Jeffery, The Foreign Vocabulary of the QurÒān; Pierre, Simon. Le stylite (esṭīūnōrō) et sa ṣawmaʿa face aux milieux cléricaux islamiques et miaphysites (Ier–IIe/VIIe–VIIIe siècles).” Al-ʿUṣīūr al-Wusṭā 28 (2020): 174–226.).
 [7] God Almighty will grant victory to those who strive in His Path to uphold His Religion and make His Word supreme. Supporting God means supporting His cause, His Messenger, and the Truth He revealed; it does not imply that He needs assistance (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī). Supporting God means following His revealed Law, obeying His Commands, refraining from what He has forbidden, supporting His Messengers and following them, defending His Religion, and striving lawfully in its defence so that His Word may be supreme (cf. al-Shinqīṭī): “You who Believe, if you support Allah, He will grant you victory and make firm your feet” (47: 7).

[1]Those who, if We establish them in the land, keep up the Prayer, give zakat [willingly],[2] enjoin virtue, and advise against what is unacceptable;[3] to Allah belongs the outcome of all affairs.[4]

[1] Having promised victory to those who support Him, God describes them in terms that show that their struggle is for His Cause, not for personal gain. After suffering persecution and expulsion from their homes—a wrong comparable in gravity to killing—if granted authority in the land, they keep up the Prayer, give zakat, enjoin virtue, and advise against what is unacceptable, thereby directing their power towards worship and obedience to God rather than self-aggrandisement (cf. al-Biqāʿī).
 [2] These are those whom God grants secure settlement and authority in the land, including victory over the Associators. They keep up the Prayer at its appointed times and with its prescribed limits, pillars, conditions, and obligations, and give zakat from their wealth to those entitled to receive it (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [3] They call people to Belief, affirmation of God’s Oneness, and obedience to Him, while warning them against Denial, Association with Him, and disobedience. The command includes opposing and restraining wrongdoing by lawful means within one’s authority and ability; “what is unacceptable” is what God’s revealed Law rejects (cf. Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, al-Ālīūsī). As a reflection on their social implications, the four qualities mentioned here express the moral and social character of a community worthy of Divine establishment. Keeping up the Prayer orders the individual’s relationship with God, cultivates discipline, humility, moral restraint, and equality, and repeatedly gathers people of different ranks before their Lord on the same footing. Giving zakat orders the community’s economic life by making wealth answerable to moral duty, protecting the poor and vulnerable, moderating the distance between social classes, and replacing indifference with mutual responsibility. Enjoining virtue preserves the values upon which communal wellbeing depends, while advising against what is unacceptable helps prevent wrongdoing from becoming normalised, publicly admired, or institutionally protected.
 [4] Every matter ultimately returns to God Alone, especially in the Hereafter, when all earthly authority disappears and creation returns to Him for reward or punishment. The statement also places the preceding promise of establishment within a moral framework: rulers who uphold God’s Commands attain a praiseworthy end, whereas those who exercise authority through tyranny and personal desire may enjoy temporary power, but their ultimate outcome is blameworthy. Although falsehood may initially prevail as a trial distinguishing the truthful from the false, the outcome of every affair belongs wholly to God, and the favourable end is for those who are Mindful (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, al-Saʿdī, al-Biqāʿī). “To Allah belongs all that is in the Heavens and Earth, and to Allah all affairs shall be returned” (3: 109).
[1]If they reject you [O Muhammad] as false, so too did the people of Nīūḥ (Noah), ʿĀd, and Thamīūd before them reject [their Messengers] as false,

[1] Having explained that the Believers were wrongfully driven from their homes, permitted them to fight, promised victory to those who support His Cause, and declared that the outcome of all affairs belongs to Him, God consoles The Prophet (ﷺ) for the rejection and other harm inflicted upon him and the Believers. The passage also returns to the religious offences of the Associators, namely their Association, denial of the Resurrection, turning people away from God’s religion and barring them from the Sacred Mosque, and expulsion of its rightful worshippers. It then likens them to earlier peoples that rejected their Messengers and suffered Divine Punishment, thereby warning them against meeting the same fate (cf. al-Rāzī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
as did the people of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and the people of Līūṭ (Lot),
and the inhabitants of Madyan; and Mīūsā (Moses) was rejected.[1] I then granted the Deniers respite, then seized them;[2] how terrible was My Chastisement![3]

[1] When the Associators of Makkah rejected the Truth brought to them, they were following the established pattern of earlier nations that rejected God’s Messengers. The Prophet (ﷺ) was not the first Messenger to be rejected: before his people, the people of Nīūḥ rejected their Messenger, ʿĀd rejected Hīūd, Thamīūd rejected Ṣāliḥ, the peoples of Ibrāhīm and Līūṭ rejected their Messengers, the people of Madyan rejected Shuʿayb, and Pharaoh and his people rejected Mīūsā. The statement supports The Prophet (ﷺ), reminding him that earlier Messengers were likewise rejected and remained patient until God’s Judgement overtook their opponents. As a result, he is called to follow their example and remain steadfast (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qāsimī, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] God Almighty did not hasten to Punish the rejecting nations when they Denied their Messengers. Rather, He allowed them a period of respite, then seized them with Punishment at the appointed time. The fate of most of these peoples is detailed elsewhere in the Qur’an (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Abī Zamanīn, al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī). The same Divine pattern is stated elsewhere: “Indeed, Messengers before you ˹Muhammad˺ were ridiculed, and I allowed the Deniers time then I took them; how was then My Punishment!” (13: 32). It is also illustrated through the different forms of Punishment that befell earlier peoples: “So We seized each ˹people˺ for their sin: against some of them We sent a storm of stones, some were overtaken by a ˹mighty˺ blast, some We caused the Earth to swallow, and some We drowned—Allah would not have treated them unjustly, but it was they who were unjust to themselves” (29: 40). Abīū Mīūsā al-Ashʿarī (رضي الله عنه) narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: “Indeed, Allah grants the wrongdoer respite, but when He seizes him, He does not let him escape.” He then recited: “Such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are doing wrong. Surely His seizing is painful, severe!” (11: 102) (al-Bukhārī: 4686; Muslim: 2583).
 [3] “How terrible was My Chastisement!” renders fa-kayfa kāna nakīr. Nakīr denotes God’s repudiation of wrongdoing, here manifested in exemplary Punishment. In this context, that Punishment also vindicates His Messengers against those who rejected them. The root n-k-r conveys the sense of something unrecognised, disapproved of, or repudiated, and the expression hence evokes a Punishment so severe that it manifests God’s utter repudiation of their deeds (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah). Ibn ʿĀshīūr explains: “Nakīr is a deterrent repudiation intended to change the condition of the person against whom it is directed. The final kasrah in nakīr in connected recitation indicates the omitted first-person possessive yāʾ, which is dropped for ease of pronunciation. The appropriateness of choosing nakīr in this aya, rather than Punishment or a similar expression, lies in its occurrence after the commendation of advising against what is unacceptable. This alerts Muslims to exert the utmost of their ability in changing what is unacceptable, for Allah punished unacceptable conduct with the severest Punishment. Believers should therefore follow the example set by Allah’s action. The sages have said: ‘Wisdom consists in resembling the Creator to the extent permitted by human capacity.’ In this arena, the finest steeds of lofty aspiration compete.” This ethical analogy concerns human conduct appropriate to the servant, within lawful authority and proportionate limits; it does not confer Divine prerogatives upon human beings.
How many a town[1] have We destroyed while it was steeped in wrongdoing, leaving it lying in ruins upon its roofs;[2] and many an abandoned well and many a [deserted] lofty palace![3]

[1] al-Shinqīṭī explains: “The word qaryah, ‘town’, is sometimes used for the buildings themselves and at other times for the people who inhabit them. Accordingly, the destruction in His Words, ‘have We destroyed’, and the wrongdoing in His Words, ‘while it was steeped in wrongdoing’, refer to its inhabitants, whereas His Words, ‘leaving it lying in ruins upon its roofs’, refer to its buildings.”
 [2] “Leaving it lying in ruins upon its roofs” means that the roofs first collapsed, then the walls fell upon them, leaving the houses completely demolished. al-Shinqīṭī considers this the most evident interpretation; another takes the expression more generally as describing deserted or ruined dwellings (cf. al-Shinqīṭī).
 [3] How many a well, although intact, still yielding water, and fit for use, was left abandoned after those who drew from it had been destroyed. Likewise, how many a palace, described by the exegetes as lofty, plastered, fortified, or well built, was emptied of its inhabitants after they had perished, becoming desolate after once being inhabited and full of life (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr): “How many a town defied the Command of its Lord and His Messengers, so We called it to a severe Reckoning and punished it with a dreadful Punishment. *It then tasted the evil consequences of its conduct, and the outcome of its affair was loss” (65: 8–9).

[1]Have they not travelled throughout the land, so that they may have hearts by which to reason,[2] or ears by which to hear? Indeed, it is not the eyes that go blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind.[3]

[1] This follows the account of the towns destroyed for rejecting their Messengers. The Quraysh knew the lands of those earlier peoples, passed by some of their ruins, and heard reports concerning their fate. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn ʿAjībah explain that travelling through the land may be physical, through personally witnessing the remains of destroyed nations, or figurative, through hearing accounts of them from others. Such travel should awaken hearts to reason from these visible Signs of God’s Oneness and Power, and ears to hear with reflection and admonition, so that people recognise the causes of success and destruction and take heed before a similar fate befalls them. Yet because neither what they saw nor what they heard produced reflection, their travelling is treated as though it had never occurred (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, al-Saʿdī, Abīū Ḥayyān, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, Ibn ʿAjībah, al-Shinqīṭī, Ibn al-Qayyim, Iʿlām al-Muwaqqiʿīn, 1: 103). “Have they not travelled throughout the land and observed how the outcome was for those before them? They were more numerous than them, mightier in strength, and left greater traces upon the land, yet what they used to earn availed them nothing” (40: 82); “Have they not travelled throughout the land and observed how the outcome was for those before them? Allah utterly destroyed them, and the Deniers shall have the like thereof” (47: 10).
 [2] “Hearts by which to reason” renders qulīūbun yaʿqilīūna bihā. The Qur’an attributes ʿaql, understanding and considered judgement, to the heart. In classical exegesis, the heart is associated with comprehension, intention, and volition; several commentators understand this as affirming a real role for the heart, not merely a figurative expression. This need not be understood as excluding the brain’s role in cognitive processes. Ibn Taymiyyah explains that the soul is connected with both the heart and the brain: thought and reflection begin in the brain, while will originates in the heart, with each affecting the other. At a different explanatory level, modern research recognises continuous interaction between cardiac activity and the brain, and indicates that cardiac signals can influence conscious perception, reward-based learning, and preference-based decision-making, without implying that the physical heart independently performs thought or establishing a scientific proof of the exegetical accounts. “Reason” thus conveys more than abstract reasoning: it indicates attentive comprehension that leads a person to reflect, recognise the Truth, and respond accordingly (cf. al-Qurṭubī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, al-Shinqīṭī, Ibn ʿUthaymīn, Ibn Taymiyyah, Majmīūʿ al-Fatāwā, 9: 303–304; Fouragnan et al., “Timing along the Cardiac Cycle Modulates Neural Signals of Reward-Based Learning”, Nature Communications 15 [2024]: 2976; Grund et al., “Respiration, Heartbeat, and Conscious Tactile Perception”, Journal of Neuroscience 42 [2022]: 643–656; Azzalini et al., “Responses to Heartbeats in Ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex Contribute to Subjective Preference-Based Decisions”, Journal of Neuroscience 41 [2021]: 5102–5114).
 [3] Their physical eyes remain capable of seeing visible things, but their hearts are blind to perceiving the Truth, comprehending its Signs, and benefiting from them. The gravest blindness is therefore not the loss of sight, but the failure or refusal to recognise what is plainly before a person and to allow that recognition to reform one’s conduct. Sight fulfils its highest spiritual purpose when it awakens reflection, humility, and obedience; otherwise, a person may see the Signs clearly yet remain inwardly blind, and this is the blindness that leads to ruin (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī): “Whoever is blind in this ˹life˺, then he is in the Hereafter ˹even˺ blinder and more astray in path” (17: 72).
[1]They urge you [challengingly, O Muhammad] to hasten the Punishment, but Allah will never fail to fulfil His Promise.[2] Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years by your reckoning.[3]

[1] Having consoled The Prophet (ﷺ) by reminding him that earlier Messengers were likewise rejected and harmed, God now exposes the depth of the Associators’ mockery and Denial: rather than fearing the Punishment of which they were warned, they repeatedly demanded that it be hastened. Accordingly, The Prophet (ﷺ) is called to remain patient and steadfast in conveying the Truth, undisturbed by their words and conduct (cf. al-Marāghī).
 [2] The Punishment God Almighty has promised the Deniers is certain to befall them at its appointed time, however long it may appear to be delayed. Some exegetes understand this promise as having been fulfilled through the defeat of the Associators and the killing of some of them at Badr, while Ibn Kathīr emphasises their coming Punishment in the Hereafter. al-Saʿdī’s broader explanation affirms the certainty of God’s promised Punishment. The two interpretations are not necessarily incompatible, since the promise may encompass both their worldly defeat and their ultimate Punishment (cf. Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, al-Khāzin, al-Maḥallī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī): “They urge you to hasten the Punishment. Were it not for an appointed term, the Punishment would surely have come upon them; and it will certainly come upon them suddenly, while they are unaware. *They urge you to hasten the Punishment, while Hell is verily surrounding the Deniers” (29: 53–54).
 [3] “Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years by your reckoning” explains why the delay of Punishment should not be mistaken for neglect or inability. God is Forbearing and grants wrongdoers respite until their appointed time, but the fulfilment of His Promise remains inevitable, and none can escape Him. al-Ṭabarī understands the statement in this contextual sense: what appears exceedingly distant to people is near to God, and the length of the delay makes no difference to His Power to seize them. Ibn Kathīr offers a similar explanation, and al-Saʿdī records it as one possible understanding, while Ibn ʿĀshīūr regards it as an implicit warning that, even if worldly Punishment is postponed, the Deniers cannot escape the more severe Punishment of the Day of Judgement. Other exegetes understand the “day” as a day of Punishment in the Hereafter, equal to a thousand worldly years, or more generally as a day of the Hereafter; another view identifies it as one of the six days in which the Heavens and the Earth were created (cf. al-Zajjāj, al-Biqāʿī, al-Qāsimī, al-Samarqandī, al-Samʿānī, al-Rāzī, Yaḥyā Ibn Sallām, Ibn al-Jawzī, Ibn Juzayy, al-Wāḥidī, Muqātil, Aḥmad Ibn Ḥanbal).
How many a town have I granted respite while it was steeped in wrongdoing, then seized it; and to Me is the final return.[1]
[1] “Indeed, to Us is their return; *then indeed, upon Us is their reckoning” (88: 25–26).
[1]Say [O Muhammad]: “O people, I am only a clarifying warner to you.”[2]

[1] Here is a merciful appeal following the preceding evidence and warnings. Calls to reflection and considered judgement are strategically distributed throughout the sura: the universal address, rendered “O mankind” or “O people”, appears in Ayas 1, 5, 49, and 73, while Aya 46 urges people to travel through the land, observe the fate of earlier nations, and understand with their hearts. Together, these passages repeatedly summon humanity to think, take heed, and respond to the Truth before Punishment overtakes them.
 [2] After the preceding admonitions and warnings, the command “Say” introduces a renewed declaration of the Prophet’s mission, while the address “O people” calls all people to attend carefully, with particular force for the immediate addressees, the Associators. Their rejection and mockery neither provoke The Prophet (ﷺ) nor deter him from conveying the Message. Rather, the statement rebukes their assumption that persistent opposition might weary him into abandoning his call, while reassuring and strengthening him. “I am only a clarifying warner to you” restricts his role in this context: he seeks neither revenge against them nor their favour. Whoever Believes does so for their own benefit, while whoever remains blind bears the consequence (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
So those who Believe and do righteous deeds shall have Forgiveness and an honourable Provision.[1]

[1] “An honourable Provision” is understood by al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, and al-Shinqīṭī as the Provision of Paradise. Muḥammad Ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī is reported by Ibn Kathīr as saying that whenever God mentions “an honourable Provision”, He means Paradise. al-Biqāʿī and Ibn ʿĀshīūr understand it more broadly as encompassing Provision in both this world and the Hereafter, whereas Ibn ʿĀshīūr takes its worldly aspect primarily as spiritual.
