Describing the Provision as “honourable” conveys its excellence and abundance; in Paradise, this also includes complete freedom from anything that might diminish or disturb its enjoyment (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī).
But those who toil laboriously[1] against Our Signs, seeking to thwart [Us],[2] those are the Companions of the Blazing Fire.

[1] “Toil laboriously” renders saʿaw. Saʿy literally means moving swiftly, but is commonly used for earnest exertion in pursuing an aim, whether good or evil. Here it describes their determined efforts to oppose, discredit, and frustrate the effect of God’s Signs (cf. al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt; Ibn Juzayy, al-Shinqīṭī).
 [2] Muʿājizīn indicates opposing, obstinately resisting, and seeking to prevail. Linguistically, muʿājazah depicts attempting to render one’s opponent incapable, with each party seeking to demonstrate the other’s inability. One fundamental sense of the root ʿ-j-z is weakness or incapacity (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-QurÒān; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Wāḥidī, al-Basīṭ; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān). The form muʿājizīn suggests active opposition in which each side seeks to render the other powerless. It may therefore describe their attempts to overpower the Prophet and his followers, obstruct the establishment of the Truth, and prevent people from accepting it. The rendering “seeking to thwart [Us]” presents their intended resistance, not an ability actually to defeat God’s Purpose. The expression may also convey their deluded belief that they could escape God’s Power and frustrate His Judgement. al-Shinqīṭī considers the first interpretation more immediately consistent with the reciprocal form, while both meanings express their hostile resistance to the Signs (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī).

[1]No Messenger or Prophet[2] did We ever send before you [O Muhammad] except that, whenever he recited,[3] Satan cast [doubts] regarding his recitation. Allah then nullifies[4] what Satan casts; thereafter Allah firmly establishes[5] His Signs;[6] Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.

[1] These ayas continue the consolation and strengthening of The Prophet (ﷺ) begun in the preceding passage. After clarifying that his responsibility is only to deliver a clear warning, and that those who Believe are saved while those who reject are ruined, the discourse explains that his experience is shared by the Messengers and Prophets (عليهم السلام) before him. None was spared Satan’s attempts to obstruct the Guidance they conveyed or to corrupt its reception among their peoples. As with earlier nations, some accepted the Truth while others rejected it, in accordance with God’s established way concerning His Messengers (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] “No Messenger or Prophet” is expressly universal, indicating that none of the Messengers or Prophets (عليهم السلام) was exempt from Satan’s attempts to obstruct the Message (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr). The coordination of “Prophet” with “Messenger” indicates that the two terms are not wholly synonymous. Scholars generally hold that every Messenger is a Prophet, but not every Prophet is a Messenger, although they differ over the precise distinction. Some maintain that a Messenger is given an independent revealed Law or Book, whereas a Prophet calls people to the Law of an earlier Messenger. Ibn Taymiyyah argues that an independent Law is not essential; rather, a Messenger is sent with a Divine Message to people who oppose or reject it, while a Prophet guides a Believing community according to an established revealed Law. The common definition of a Prophet as one who receives Revelation but is not commanded to convey it is difficult to sustain, since this aya expressly describes both Prophets and Messengers as being sent (cf. al-Qurṭubī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī, Ibn Taymiyyah, al-Nubuwwāt, 2: 718).
 [3] “Whenever he recited” renders idhā tamannā, while “his recitation” renders umniyyatihi. Here tamannā is understood as reciting or reading Revelation. The root m-n-y conveys the measuring or determining of something, and recitation is associated with this sense because each aya is ordered and placed in its proper position. Another interpretation retains the familiar meaning of tamannā, “to wish”, referring to a Prophet’s earnest desire for his people to accept Guidance. The first interpretation accords more directly with the immediate reference to what Satan casts in relation to the Prophetic recitation (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-QurÒān; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; al-Shinqīṭī). This aya has generated considerable disagreement among exegetes. The interpretation adopted in the translation is that whenever a Messenger or Prophet recited Revelation, Satan sought to interfere with its reception by casting doubts, insinuations, and misleading suggestions into the minds of the hearers, so as to turn them away from what was being recited (cf. al-Tafsīr al-Muyassar). The statement does not require that Satan inserted anything into the Revelation itself; rather, his interference concerned people’s hearing and understanding of the Prophetic recitation. God then nullifies what Satan casts and firmly establishes His Signs. Most early exegetes, including Mujāhid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and many later authorities understand tamannā here as “recited”, and umniyyatihi as “his recitation”. A second interpretation takes tamannā in its familiar sense of wishing, namely, a Prophet’s earnest desire that his people accept Guidance, with Satan seeking to obstruct that desire through doubts and opposition. Some exegetes combine both meanings: the Prophet recites the Revelation while sincerely desiring that his people Believe. Those who understand tamannā as recitation then differ over the nature of Satan’s interference. One view, preferred by al-Shinqīṭī, is that Satan casts doubts, insinuations, and false descriptions of the Revelation into the minds of its hearers, claiming, for example, that it is sorcery, poetry, or fabricated tales. On this reading, nothing is inserted into the Revelation itself. Another view, attributed by Ibn Taymiyyah to many of the early scholars, understands the casting as occurring in connection with the recitation itself, while maintaining that God immediately annuls whatever Satan casts and firmly establishes His Signs, so that no falsehood remains in the settled transmission of Revelation. In either case, the aya affirms the Prophets’ protection in conveying God’s Message and explains that Satanic interference becomes a trial for diseased and hardened hearts, while people of Knowledge recognise the Truth more firmly. The so-called gharānīq report, often called the story of the “Satanic verses”, alleges that words praising the Makkan deities were heard during the recitation of Sīūrat al-Najm. Ibn Kathīr states that he knew of no sound, connected chain for it; other authorities likewise rejected its reliability. Some scholars nevertheless regarded the multiple disconnected reports as supporting a historical basis, while differing over what occurred. One explanation attributes the words to Satan and the Associators’ mistaken hearing, not to The Prophet (ﷺ). Because of this, the report cannot be presented as an established account that the Prophet uttered false words as part of the Qur’an. The aya itself affirms that God nullifies Satanic interference and firmly establishes His Signs (cf. al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Shinqīṭī, Ibn Taymiyyah, Majmīūʿ al-Fatāwā, 15: 190–191).
 [4] “Nullifies” renders yansakhu. Here naskh means to abolish, remove, or render ineffective what Satan casts. The root n-s-kh includes removal or supersession, as well as transfer or copying; replacement is not required in every use. As such, God eliminates the effect of Satan’s insinuations, then firmly establishes His Signs (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb).
 [5] “Firmly establishes” renders yuḥkimu, which refers to making firm and secure; purification from falsehood is its contextual explanation. The root ḥ-k-m fundamentally denotes restraint or prevention (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Samʿānī, Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah). God is All-Knowing of everything that occurs among His creation, including what He reveals to His Prophet and what Satan casts. He is All-Wise in everything He does, placing each thing in its proper and fitting place. Part of His Wisdom lies in allowing Satan to cast falsehood, without approving it, and in exposing and nullifying it while preserving His Revelation (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Nasafī, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿAjībah, al-Alīūsī, al-Saʿdī).
 [6] On the interpretation adopted here, God nullifies Satanic doubts concerning the Signs of His Book, preserves and firmly establishes them, and makes manifest that they are Revelation truly sent down from Him. Satan’s attempts to turn people away from them cannot affect their Divine Truth or integrity (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Nasafī, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī).
[He allows this][1] so as to make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is disease and those whose hearts are hardened;[2] verily, the wrongdoers are in deep-seated opposition.[3]

[1] Out of His perfect Wisdom, God allows Satanic doubts to become a trial, without approving their falsehood, for those whose hearts harbour spiritual disease, explained as doubt, hypocrisy, or Denial, and for the hard-hearted, identified in this context with the Associators, who neither soften to the Truth nor return to what is right (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Makkī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, al-Shawkānī, al-ʿUlaymī): “He ˹Allah˺ misguides with it ˹this example˺ a great number of people and guides with it a great number of people. But He only misguides the Transgressors” (2: 26); “Like so We made for every Prophet an enemy, the devils of humans and jinn; they inspire each other with glittering speech in order to deceive, had your Lord wished, they would not have done so; leave them then and their ˹false˺ fabrications. *And that the hearts of those who do not Believe in the Hereafter may be drawn to it ˹such deceit˺, and they may approve of it and ˹insistently˺ perpetrate what they are perpetrating” (6: 112–113).
 [2] These ayas distinguish three states of the heart: two hearts overcome by trial and one saved heart. The diseased heart is weak and unstable, unable to retain the Truth firmly; the hardened heart is dry and unresponsive, neither accepting the Truth nor submitting to it. The Believing, humbly submissive, tranquil heart, by contrast, receives the Truth of the Qur’an and is strengthened by it. Ibn al-Qayyim explains that the sound heart needs only to perceive the Truth in order to love, prefer, and follow it. The dead, hardened heart neither accepts nor submits, while the diseased heart inclines towards whichever of health or sickness prevails within it. What Satan casts consequently becomes a trial for the diseased and hardened hearts, but strengthens the living, sound heart, which rejects falsehood, submits more fully to the Truth, and increases in faith and love of it (cf. Ibn al-Qayyim, Shifāʾ al-ʿAlīl, discussion of 22: 53; Ighāthat al-Lahfān, 1: 10).
 [3] “The wrongdoers” encompasses the two preceding groups, those with diseased hearts and those with hardened hearts. They are entrenched in opposition and defiance of God’s Command and are far removed from the Truth and what is right. Their ẓulm consists particularly in rejecting and resisting the Truth, and, according to the different identifications of these groups, may encompass Denial, Association, hypocrisy, or obstinate opposition to God’s Command (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).

And so that those who were given knowledge[1] may know that it is the Truth from your Lord, then Believe in it, and then their hearts humbly submit to it;[2] verily, Allah surely will guide those who Believe to a Straight Path.[3]

[1] They are those whom God has granted beneficial Knowledge, by which they distinguish Truth from falsehood and recognise that the Revelation God has sent down is the Truth, unlike what Satan casts (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] The three verbs, “know”, “Believe”, and “humbly submit”, mark a deliberate progression: beneficial Knowledge here strengthens Belief, and Belief leads to the heart’s humble submission. The two occurrences of fa- convey consequence and close succession: once they recognise the Revelation as the Truth, they Believe in it, whereupon their hearts submit to it.
 [3] God Almighty guides the Believers to the path of Truth, enables them to follow it, and helps them avoid falsehood, so that Satan’s schemes and insinuations do not harm them. This Guidance extends to both worlds: in this life, He directs them to recognise and follow the Truth and to reject falsehood; in the Hereafter, He guides them along the path leading to the ranks of Paradise and delivers them from the painful Punishment (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Samʿānī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī).

Yet the Deniers will persist in [lingering] doubt[1] concerning it (the Qur’an)[2] until the Hour comes upon them suddenly [and without warning],[3] or the Punishment of a barren[4] Day comes upon them.

[1] “[Lingering] doubt” renders miryah. Miryah implies doubt; al-Rāghib more specifically defines it as wavering concerning a matter and distinguishes it from the broader shakk. The continuing sense conveyed by “[lingering]” comes from the construction lā yazālīūna, “will persist”, rather than the noun alone (cf. al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān).
 [2] The same revealed Truth is received differently according to the condition of the heart. The sound, humble heart recognises it, Believes in it, and submits to it; the diseased heart encounters it but responds with wavering doubt, while the hardened heart rejects it with obstinate resistance. The Deniers’ continued miryah hence arises not from any obscurity in the Revelation, but from the sickness and hardness of their hearts. Ibn al-Qayyim explains that Satan’s doubts become a trial for these two hearts, whereas the living, sound heart recognises those doubts as false and thereby increases in certainty, submission, and love of the Truth (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, Ibn al-Qayyim, Shifāʾ al-ʿAlīl, discussion of 22: 53; Ighāthat al-Lahfān, 1: 10).
 [3] “Suddenly [and without warning]” renders baghtatan. The word stands for something arriving abruptly and unexpectedly, from a direction or at a time the person does not anticipate (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-QurÒān; al-Zajjāj, Maʿānī al-QurÒān; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt; al-Kafawī, al-Kulliyyāt). The Hour will arrive abruptly and unexpectedly, leaving people no opportunity to complete even the ordinary acts in which they are engaged. As Allah says: “It will come to you naught but all of a sudden” (7: 187). Abīū Hurayrah (رضي الله عنه) related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: “The Hour will not come until the sun rises from where it sets [the West]. When it rises thus, people will see it and they will all then Believe, and that is when: ‘…a soul’s Believing will be to no avail to it had it not Believed earlier or earned good in its Believing…’ (6: 158). Verily, the Hour will surely come [suddenly] while two men are spreading a cloth between them; they will not be given time to finish their bargain or to fold the cloth. Verily, the Hour will surely come [suddenly] while a man is still carrying the milk he obtained from his she-camel, but he will not be able to taste it. Verily, the Hour will surely come [suddenly] while a man is repairing his watering trough, and he will not have time to water [his herd] from it. Verily, the Hour will surely come [suddenly] while a person raises a morsel of food to his mouth, but he will not be able to eat it” (al-Bukhārī: 6506; cf. Muslim: 157 for the sun rising from the west).
 [4] “A barren Day” equates to yawmin ʿaqīm. Many exegetes understand it as the Day of Judgement, called “barren” because it ends the familiar succession of worldly days and nights and because it yields no good, relief, or further opportunity for the Deniers. This interpretation is supported by the following statement: “On that Day, All Dominion belongs to Allah; He will judge between them.” Another well-attested interpretation, preferred by al-Ṭabarī and Ibn ʿĀshīūr, identifies it as the Day of Badr, which was barren of all joy and relief for the Deniers, many of whom were killed before evening. Ibn Kathīr and al-Shinqīṭī consider the Day of Judgement the more contextually evident meaning, while acknowledging that Badr formed part of the Punishment promised to them (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, al-Qurṭubī, al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Shawkānī, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī).
On that Day, All Dominion belongs to Allah; He will judge between them. So those who Believe and do righteous deeds will be in Gardens of Bliss.[1]

[1] Abīū Hurayrah (رضي الله عنه) related that The Prophet (ﷺ) said: “Allah says: ‘I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has ever seen, no ear has ever heard, and what no human heart has ever conceived’” (al-Bukhārī: 3244, 7498; Muslim: 2824). In parallel narrations, Abīū Hurayrah (رضي الله عنه) related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: “The first group to enter Paradise will be as radiant as the full moon, and those following them will be like the brightest star in the sky. They will neither urinate nor defecate, neither spit nor blow their noses. Their combs will be of gold, their sweat will be fragrant like musk, and aloeswood will burn in their incense burners. Their spouses will be the wide-eyed maidens of Paradise. They will be of one harmonious disposition, with neither disagreement nor hatred among them, and they will glorify Allah morning and evening” (al-Bukhārī: 3245, 3327; Muslim: 2834).
But those who Denied and declared Our Signs false, those shall have a humiliating Punishment.[1]

[1] ʿAmr Ibn Shuʿayb related through his father, from his grandfather, ʿAbdullāh Ibn ʿAmr, that The Prophet (ﷺ) said: “The arrogant will be gathered on the Day of Judgement like tiny ants in human form, with humiliation enveloping them from every direction. They will be driven to a prison in Hell called Bīūlas. The Fire of fires will rise over them, and they will be given to drink from the putrid discharge of the inhabitants of the Fire, known as the mire of corruption (ṭīnat al-khabāl)” (al-Tirmidhī: 2492; Aḥmad: 6677).
[1]And those who migrated in the Path of Allah, and were then killed or died, Allah will surely provide them with a comely Provision;[2] verily, Allah surely is the Best of Providers.[3]

[1] The following ayas return to the Believers who were driven from their homes and granted permission to defend themselves after suffering persecution. They first assure those who migrated in Allah’s Path that their reward is secure, whether they were killed or died naturally, for both migrated sincerely in God’s Path and sacrificed their former homes for His Cause. God promises them a satisfying Provision and an entrance with which they will be entirely pleased. Most exegetes understand this as their entrance into Paradise, while al-Saʿdī also includes the lands opened to them, particularly their joyful and victorious return to Makkah after having been expelled from it. The wording may thus encompass both their worldly vindication and their final reward in the Hereafter. The passage then turns from promise to action: those who have been wronged may defend themselves and respond to aggression only in equal measure, without excess. If their aggressors renew the injustice after such a proportionate response, God promises to support the wronged. In the wider context of the sura, this links the emigrants’ promised return and victory with the earlier permission to fight, the restoration of access to the Sacred Mosque, and the establishment of the religion and its rites. al-Ṭabarī understands the concluding Divine Names, “All-Pardoning, Most Forgiving”, as assuring the wronged that lawful equivalent requital incurs no punishment. al-Saʿdī additionally draws encouragement to pardon, whereas Ibn ʿĀshīūr connects the Names here with limiting requital to strict equivalence (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] “Comely Provision” refers primarily to the noble Provision of Paradise, as understood by al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Suddī. An interpretation attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās explains it as lawful provision, while al-Saʿdī takes the promise more broadly to include abundant Provision in this world as well as the Hereafter. Those who leave their homes, families, and possessions seeking God’s Pleasure are therefore assured that they will not be deprived, whether they are killed or die naturally. This promise was fulfilled for the early emigrants when God opened lands to them and granted them abundance after they had sacrificed their former homes and wealth for His religion (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī): “Do not think that those who got killed in the cause of Allah are dead. Nay but they are alive with their Lord [being handsomely] provided for” (3: 169); “Those who migrated, were expelled from their lands, persecuted in My cause, fought and got killed, I shall expunge their misdeeds and admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow; a reward from Allah—indeed with Allah is the best of rewards” (3: 195); and “Whoever sets out from his home migrating to Allah and His Messenger, but death catches up with him, his reward is securely assured by Allah” (4: 100). Salmān al-Fārisī (رضي الله عنه) narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: “Keeping watch for a day and a night [on the frontier in Allah’s Path] is better than fasting for a month and standing in Prayer throughout its nights. If a person dies while keeping watch, the reward for the deed he had been performing will continue to be credited to him, his Provision will continue to be granted to him, and he will be kept safe from the trial [of the grave]” (Muslim: 1913).
 [3] al-Biqāʿī says: “‘Allah surely is the Best of Providers’: He provides for all creation, the righteous and the wicked alike, so how much more will He provide for one who migrates to Him? He bestows a bounty beyond all count or limit.” (Naẓm al-Durar, commentary on 22: 58).
He will surely grant them an entrance[1] that will please them; verily, Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing.

[1] “An entrance” corresponds to mudkhalan. The word may represent either the place into which someone is admitted or the act of admitting them. Entry is the opposite of exit and may be used in relation to places, times, and deeds (cf. al-Wāḥidī, al-Basīṭ; al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt; Ibn ʿĀshīūr). Most exegetes understand the promised entrance as Paradise, where they will encounter blessings beyond all human perception. al-Saʿdī, however, understands the wording more broadly as encompassing both the lands opened to the emigrants, particularly their joyful entrance into Makkah, and their ultimate entrance into Paradise. (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Alīūsī, al-Saʿdī).
[1]That is so; whoever punishes with the like of what he was punished,[2] and is then aggressed against anew, Allah will surely grant him victory; verily, Allah is All-Pardoning, Most Forgiving.[3]

[1] Dhālika (That is so) marks a transition between the preceding promise to the emigrants and the renewed discussion of resistance to aggression. The demonstrative draws the hearers’ attention to the importance of what follows and stands independently of the following clause, “whoever punishes”; the two do not form a subject–predicate construction. The passage thus resumes the theme introduced in Ayas 39–40, where those who had been wronged were granted permission to fight and promised Divine support. “Whoever punishes” is expressed in the singular to formulate a general rule applicable to individuals and communities alike (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr). According to al-Zajjāj, “That is so” refers back to the preceding promise that God will fulfil His pledge to the emigrants, whether they are killed or die. In contrast, al-Biqāʿī understands the expression as confirming the preceding description of God as All-Knowing, Most Forbearing.
 [2] The original persecution of the Believers is described as “punishment” because the Associators intended thereby to punish them for abandoning Association and rejecting the worship of idols. Their aggression included harming the Muslims and forcing them from their homeland. On account of this, the Believers were permitted to respond in kind, but only proportionately and without excess. In this context, such a response could include fighting those who had expelled them and restoring their access to their homeland. The translation adopts the understanding, supported by al-Saʿdī, that the aggressors then renew their aggression. Ibn ʿĀshīūr instead understands thumma as a rhetorical progression emphasising that the Believers were subjected to aggression, without requiring a subsequent attack (cf. al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [3] al-Saʿdī explains that God continually deals with His servants with pardon and forgiveness. Those who have been wronged should therefore pardon, overlook, and forgive, so that God may deal with them as they deal with His servants (cf. al-Saʿdī): “Whoever pardons and sets things right, his reward is with Allah” (42: 40).
[1]That is so because Allah merges night into day and merges day into night, and because Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.

[1] These ayas explain why God’s promise of victory to the wronged Believers is certain. Ibn ʿĀshīūr understands the merging of night into day and day into night as a cosmic image of one opposing force gaining ascendancy over another. Just as the periods of light and darkness alternate and neither remains permanently dominant, God can reverse human conditions, making the defeated victorious and the dominant defeated. The imagery may also intimate the emergence of the light of Belief and the true religion after the darkness of Denial and Association. God’s Power to govern these vast opposing forces thereby demonstrates His absolute Ability to establish the Believers’ cause and overcome their oppressors. The Divine Names “All-Hearing, All-Seeing” assure the Believers that God hears all they say, including their supplications, and sees their suffering, steadfastness, and deeds, just as He hears and sees the words and aggression of the Deniers. His promised support is therefore granted with perfect Knowledge and Wisdom. “Allah is the Truth” means that He Alone is the true God and the only One worthy of worship; consequently, the religion He has revealed and the promise He has made are true and will ultimately be established. Whatever the Associators invoke besides Him is falsehood, powerless to benefit, harm, or prevent His Decree. As “the Most High, the Supremely Great”, He is exalted above all creation and possesses complete Power and Dominion over all things (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
That is so[1] because Allah is the Truth, what they invoke besides Him is falsehood itself, and Allah is the Most High, the Supremely Great.

[1] The repeated “That is so” may be read as forming a deliberate progression. In Ayas 61–62, bi-anna, “because”, explicitly introduces the causal explanation; Aya 60 has the independent demonstrative dhālika. In Aya 60, it confirms the preceding promise to the emigrants and marks a transition to the principle of proportionate defence and the promise of victory. In Aya 61, it points back to that promised victory and grounds it in a visible Sign of God’s Power: just as He causes night and day to prevail over one another, He can reverse the balance between the oppressed and their oppressors. In Aya 62, the expression introduces the ultimate foundation of that Power and victory: Allah Alone is the Truth, whatever is invoked besides Him is falsehood, and He is the Most High, the Supremely Great. In this way, the sequence moves from confirming the promise, to demonstrating God’s Ability to fulfil it, to grounding both promise and Power in His exclusive Divinity (cf. al-Zajjāj, al-Shawkānī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
[1]Do you not see[2] that Allah sends water down from the sky, whereupon the land becomes green?[3] Verily, Allah is All-Subtle, All-Aware.[4]

[1] In a thematic reading, the following Signs of God’s Power and Beneficence prepare for the reference to the prescribed rite. The One Who sends down rain, brings the Earth to life, owns all that is in the Heavens and on the Earth, makes what is on Earth and ships at sea serviceable to humanity, and gives life, death, and resurrection is Alone entitled to prescribe the manner in which He is worshipped. Hence, the Associators have no right to dispute with The Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the rite ordained for his community. The statement also returns to the earlier discussion of the rites of pilgrimage in Aya 34, after the intervening promise that God will defend, support, and grant victory to the wronged Believers. In the wider context of the sura, these manifestations of Divine Power may further intimate that the One Who transforms the Earth and governs creation is fully Able to reverse the Believers’ condition, restore their access to the Sacred House, and enable them to establish the rites from which they had been barred (cf. al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] See footnote to Aya 18 above. Ibn ʿĀshīūr holds that the address is directed to anyone capable of seeing, since what is referred to is something well known and readily observable. Another view is that the address is specifically to The Prophet (ﷺ) (cf. al-Ṭabarī).
 [3] “Among His Signs is that you see the land devoid of life, but as soon as We send down rain upon it, it begins to stir [to life] and swell. Indeed, the One Who revives it will surely revive the dead; He is certainly Most Able over all things” (41: 39); “We send blessed water down from the sky and grow with it gardens, grain for harvest, *and soaring palm trees, with clustered dates; *a provision for the servants, and We give life with it to the land which is dead. Such is the coming forth [resurrection]” (50: 9–11).
 [4] God is All-Subtle in bringing about whatever He Wills, including causing the land to grow through water, and He is All-Aware, knowing the hidden realities of everything. Even a seed concealed beneath the earth does not escape His Knowledge; in His subtle care, He directs water to it so that it may grow (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī).
To Him belongs whatever is in the Heavens and whatever is on the Earth; verily, Allah surely is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.[1]

[1] God is utterly Self-Sufficient, needing nothing whatsoever, and He is Praiseworthy in His Names, Attributes, and Acts. al-Saʿdī expresses the relationship between the two Names succinctly: He is Self-Sufficient in His Praise and Praiseworthy in His Self-Sufficiency (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī).

Do you not see that Allah has subjected to you whatever is on the Earth[1] and the ships which sail upon the sea by His Command;[2] and He holds the sky lest it fall upon the Earth except by His Permission?[3] Verily, Allah surely is Most Compassionate, Most Merciful towards people.[4]

[1] God Almighty has made serviceable to humanity all that is on the Earth, including animals, trees, and rivers, and has made their various benefits available to humans (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] God has made the ships serviceable to you, enabling them by His Power and facilitation to sail across the seas, carrying you and your goods from one place to another (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī).
 [3] God holds the sky by His Power, preventing it from falling upon the Earth and destroying those upon it, unless He permits it to fall. Some exegetes understand “except by His Permission” as referring to the Day of Judgement, when the present order of the sky will be disrupted; others take it as an implicit warning that, were God to permit portions of it to fall upon them, they would inevitably do so (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Shinqīṭī, Abīū Ḥayyān, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [4] God is full of Compassion and Mercy towards people. Among the manifestations of these Attributes is that He has subjected all these things for their benefit and prevents the sky from falling upon the Earth and destroying those upon it (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī).
He is the One Who gave you life, then causes you to die, then will give you life [again];[1] verily, humankind are ever ungrateful.[2]

[1] This is yet another manifestation of God Almighty’s infinite Ability and His complete control over human life and destiny. He is the One Who brought people into existence from nothing, causes them to die when their appointed terms come to an end, and will then bring them back to life on the Day of Judgement for reckoning and recompense. Human life, death, and ultimate destiny are therefore entirely under His Dominion. The One Who originated life in the first place is surely Able to restore it after death (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī): “Say: ‘Allah gives you life, then causes you to die, then will gather you on the Day of Judgement, concerning which there is no doubt’” (45: 26).
 [2] The description of the human being as profoundly ungrateful points to a close connection between ingratitude and Denial. Despite the succession of manifest Signs and blessings just mentioned, some people fail to recognise the Giver behind the gifts; becoming insensible to His favours, they neither thank Him nor devote worship sincerely to Him Alone. Such ingratitude thereby lies beneath much of their rejection of His Signs: when Divine blessings cease to awaken recognition and gratitude, the heart becomes more readily disposed to Denial (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī).

For every community We have appointed a rite[1] which they [are to] observe; so let them not dispute with you [O Muhammad] concerning the matter.[2] [3]Call [people, O Muhammad] to your Lord; verily, you are surely upon straight Guidance.

[1] The word mansak (rite) is interpreted in several closely related ways. Many exegetes understand it broadly as a prescribed law, mode of worship, or religious way appointed for each community. al-Rāzī considers this the stronger interpretation, since mansak derives from nusuk, “worship”, and need not be restricted to sacrifice; the rites of Hajj as a whole are likewise called manāsik. al-Saʿdī similarly understands it as a place and form of worship appointed for every community, while al-Qāsimī glosses it as both a prescribed law and a mode of worship. al-Shinqīṭī takes the expression to mean a place in which worship is performed; within the general meaning of worship, sacrifice constitutes one particular manifestation explicitly mentioned elsewhere in the sura. al-Ṭabarī, however, understands it here more specifically as the ritual slaughter performed during the days of sacrifice at Minā, in view of the dispute with the Associators concerning such rites. Ibn ʿĀshīūr understands it as referring here to the places of the Hajj rites. The translation “rite” gives a concise contextual rendering, while these interpretations explain the term’s broader and more specific applications (cf. al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī, al-Qāsimī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] “Let them not dispute with you concerning the matter” means that The Prophet (ﷺ) is not to be diverted by their contention over the religion and the rites God has prescribed. Some exegetes understand the command as a prohibition addressed effectively to the Associators: they are not to challenge The Prophet (ﷺ) concerning matters of religion while lacking true knowledge. Others understand it as an instruction to The Prophet (ﷺ) not to give heed to their disputation or allow it to turn him away from the Truth. al-Ṭabarī relates it more specifically to their dispute concerning sacrificial slaughter, while al-Qāsimī takes it more broadly as an objection to the diversity of revealed laws among different communities or as the claim that the Prophet’s revealed Law was unnecessary because earlier laws already existed. Ibn Kathīr emphasises the practical consequence: their disputation must not affect The Prophet (ﷺ) or divert him from the clear, straight way upon which he stands (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qāsimī): “So be patient; verily, Allah’s Promise is true. And let not those who have no certainty cause you to waver” (30: 60); “Then We set you [O Muhammad] upon a prescribed Law concerning the matter; so follow it, and do not follow the desires of those who do not know” (45: 18).
 [3] “Call [people, O Muhammad] to your Lord” follows the command not to be drawn into fruitless disputation. The Prophet (ﷺ) is instead commanded to persist in calling people to God and not to regard the mere establishment of the proof as sufficient, for obstinate resistance does not necessarily yield to argument, whereas continued invitation remains beneficial to people. The omission of the object of “call” gives the command a general scope, embracing all people. “You are surely upon straight Guidance” provides the reason for such perseverance and reassures The Prophet (ﷺ) of the firmness of his course. The preposition “upon” suggests being firmly established upon Guidance, while describing that Guidance as “straight” evokes a straight road reaching its destination by the most direct route. The statement thus strengthens and encourages The Prophet (ﷺ) to continue bearing the responsibilities of his mission (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
[1]Should they argue with you, say: “Allah Knows best what you do.”

[1] If they persist in disputing with The Prophet (ﷺ), despite the proofs that should have brought the dispute to an end, he is instructed not to be drawn into further fruitless argument, but to entrust their affair to God and say: “Allah Knows best what you do.” The statement brings the disputation to a close while carrying an implicit warning: God fully knows their Denial, rejection, and the various forms of false argument by which they seek to defeat the Truth, and He will recompense them accordingly. The following statement, “Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which you used to differ”, is not part of what The Prophet (ﷺ) is commanded to say, but a fresh Divine statement intended to strengthen and reassure him and the Believers. The disagreement referred to is the same religious “matter” concerning which they had been disputing in the preceding aya; its final judgement is left to God on the Day of Judgement (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī).
Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection concerning that over which you used to differ.[1]

[1] “So to that call [people], and remain steadfast as you have been commanded; do not follow their whims, and say: ‘I Believe in whatever Book Allah has sent down, and I have been commanded to deal justly between you. Allah is our Lord and your Lord; our deeds are ours and your deeds are yours. There is no argument between us and you. Allah will gather us together, and to Him is the final return’” (42: 15).
Do you [Muhammad] not know that Allah Knows whatever is in the Heavens and the Earth?[1] Verily, that is in a Book;[2] verily, that is easy for Allah.

[1] The interrogative may be understood as either rhetorical or confirmatory, meaning you certainly know this. The statement also consoles The Prophet (ﷺ), reassuring him not to be distressed by what he encounters from them. “Verily, that is in a Book” further explains the preceding statement: God Knows all that is in the Heavens and the Earth with complete and precise Knowledge, with no loss or discrepancy. Ibn ʿĀshīūr allows “a Book” to denote either this perfect preservation figuratively or a real register appropriate to the unseen realm (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] God Knows everything that occurs in the Heavens and on the Earth and has recorded its decrees in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfīūẓ) (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī): “Every small and great [deed] is recorded” (54: 53). ʿAbdullāh Ibn ʿAmr Ibn al-ʿĀṣ (رضي الله عنهما) narrated that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: “Allah wrote the decrees of all creation fifty thousand years before He created the Heavens and the Earth” (Muslim: 2653).
[1]Yet they worship besides Allah that for which He has sent down no authority and of which they have no knowledge;[2] and the wrongdoers shall have no helper.[3]

[1] This sequence further reveals the contradiction at the heart of their disputation. God will ultimately judge between them with complete Knowledge, yet they continue to worship what rests on neither revealed authority nor true knowledge. When His clear Signs are recited to them, however, their inward rejection becomes visible on their faces and nearly bursts into violence against those who recite them. Ibn ʿĀshīūr observes that Aya 71 may depict their very state while disputing with The Prophet (ﷺ), while Aya 72 adds to their idolatry the further offences of rejecting the Messenger and the Qur’an. The contrast is therefore stark: they practise worship without Divine authority or knowledge, yet meet manifest Signs and clear proof with hostility. No helper, including their objects of worship, will save them, and the warning of the Fire brings the passage back to the Judgement already announced.
 [2] “Indeed, they follow nothing but ˹mere˺ fancies, indeed they are only guessing” (10: 66). “They are none but mere names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority; they follow naught but conjecture and that which their souls desire, though guidance has surely come to them from their Lord” (53: 23).
 [3] Because of their wrongdoing, namely their Denial and Association, the Associators will have no helper to support them, save them from God’s Punishment, or ward it off from them. The description “wrongdoers” indicates that their wrongdoing itself is the reason they will be left without support. Their worship of idols is thereby shown to be utterly futile: they worshipped them hoping for aid, yet those idols will be powerless to help them in any way (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).

When Our clear Signs are recited to them, you can recognise the look of aversion on the faces[1] of those who Deny; they nearly set upon[2] those who recite Our Signs to them. Say: “Shall I tell you of something worse than that?[3] The Fire! Allah has promised it to those who Deny; and wretched is the destination!”

[1] “The look of aversion” renders al-munkar. The word may imply either something visibly objectionable or the very act of rejection. In either case, the meaning is that signs of hatred, anger, and hostile intent become plainly visible on their faces when the Qur’an is recited to them and they are called to Believe. Their inward rejection and rage are so intense that their effects break through to their outward appearance; the expression depicts an inner state becoming unmistakably legible on the face (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] “They nearly set upon” represents yakādīūna yasṭīūna. The verb yasṭīūna denotes violently setting upon or seizing someone, particularly with the hand raised to strike. Its root, s-ṭ-w, carries the sense of overpowering and dominance. The expression therefore portrays their anger as reaching the point where they are almost ready to assault those reciting God’s Signs to them (cf. al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt; Ibn al-Jawzī, Tadhkirat al-Arīb; Ibn al-Hāʾim, al-Tibyān). The Associators are depicted as being on the verge of attacking those who recite the Qur’an to them, threatening them with harm by hand and tongue because of their intense hatred of God’s Signs and of the Truth to which they call. “Those who recite” may refer specifically to The Prophet (ﷺ), with the plural used for a single person, or more generally to The Prophet (ﷺ) and other Muslims who recited the Qur’an to them (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿālibī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). As a moral reflection, their hostility to clear Truth may be understood in light of what accepting it would demand of them. The Truth challenges inherited falsehoods, exposes self-deception, and requires the surrender of pride, desire, and entrenched interests. Hence, their aversion grows so intense that what begins as inward rejection appears visibly on their faces and almost erupts into violence against those who proclaim it. When a heart becomes attached to falsehood, clear evidence may provoke resentment rather than submission: “Grievous to the Associators is that to which you call them” (42: 13); “We have indeed brought you the Truth, but most of you are averse to the Truth” (43: 78).
 [3] “Shall I tell you of something worse than that?” means: shall I tell you of something even more grievous and hateful to you than what you have just heard? According to many exegetes, “that” (dhālikum) refers to the Qur’an whose recitation they so deeply resent; what is worse for them is the Fire that God has promised the Deniers on the Day of Judgement. Other interpretations take “that” to refer to those reciting the Qur’an, or to the assault they were on the verge of committing against them. In every case, the statement turns their present anger back upon them: however unbearable they find the Truth and its recitation, the Fire awaiting those who persist in Denial is immeasurably worse (cf. al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Rasʿanī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Ṭabarī).

[1]O mankind, a parable is set forth,[2] so listen attentively to it: [3]verily, those whom you invoke besides Allah will never create even a fly,[4] even if they all gather together for it; and if the fly snatches[5] something from them, they cannot recover it from it;[6] weak are both the seeker and the sought.[7]

[1] Having stated that the Deniers worship objects for whose worship they possess neither revealed nor rational proof, while abandoning the worship of the One Who created them, God now exposes the utter impotence of those objects of worship: they cannot create even a creature as small and weak as a fly, nor can they recover what that feeble creature takes from them. The parable thus brings together, in a single vivid image, the many arguments, admonitions, and warnings throughout the sura, establishing that God Alone is worthy of worship and that whatever is worshipped besides Him is falsehood. This prepares for the sura’s conclusion through two complementary addresses. The first, beginning “O mankind”, confronts humanity, and particularly the Deniers and Associators, with the helplessness of false objects of worship and the incomparable Power and Majesty of God, then affirms His exclusive selection of Messengers, His complete Knowledge, and the return of all affairs to Him. The second, beginning “O you who Believe”, turns to the Believers and sets out the response demanded by that recognition: humble worship, righteous action, striving in God’s cause, steadfast adherence to the religion of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), and holding firmly to God. The sura therefore concludes by moving from the exposure of false worship to the positive fulfilment of true servanthood (cf. Abīū Ḥayyān, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] The passive expression “a parable is set forth” has been understood in two ways. According to one interpretation, God sets forth the parable (mathal) to expose the utter weakness of the idols and those who worship them. According to another, the Associators themselves have, in effect, set forth a false comparison (mathal) by making their idols counterparts to God and worshipping them alongside Him. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah records both interpretations, while the first is adopted in substance by Ibn Juzayy, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Saʿdī, and the second by al-Ṭabarī, al-Samʿānī, and al-Baghawī.
 [3] Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Ṣawāʿiq al-Mursalah, 2: 466–467) draws attention to the extraordinary force and concision of this parable. Even if all the false gods were to combine their efforts, they could not create a single fly; indeed, they are so utterly powerless that they cannot even recover what a fly takes from them. On Ibn al-Qayyim’s interpretation, “the seeker” is the worshipper seeking benefit from his object of worship, while “the sought” is that helpless object itself. For that reason, the parable demolishes Association at its root: how can beings incapable of creating a creature as weak as a fly, or even recovering what it takes from them, be associated in worship with the All-Powerful, All-Prevailing? In a few vivid words, the aya establishes the argument for Divine Oneness and exposes both the weakness of false gods and the folly of those who worship them.
 [4] Abīū Hurayrah (رضي الله عنه) narrated: I heard The Prophet (ﷺ) say: “Allah (سبحانه وتعالى) said: ‘Who is more unjust than one who attempts to create like My creation? Let them then create an ant, or let them create a grain or a grain of barley!’” (al-Bukhārī: 7559; Muslim: 2111).
 [5] “Snatches” means yaslub. The verb symbolises taking something away from another by force or swiftly seizing it. al-Rāghib emphasises forcible removal, while Ibn Fāris explains the root s-l-b through swift snatching (cf. al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt; Ibn Juzayy, Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah).
 [6] Ibn al-Jawzī relates from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Associators used to coat their idols with saffron; once it dried, flies would come and snatch some of it away. He also relates from Ibn Jurayj that when they perfumed their idols, they would mix the perfume with something sweet, such as honey, whereupon flies would settle on them and carry some of it away, while neither the supposed gods nor their worshippers could prevent the flies from doing so.
 [7] “Weak are both the seeker and the sought” has been interpreted in several ways. According to the interpretation transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās and preferred by al-Ṭabarī, “the seeker” is the idol, powerless to recover what has been snatched from it, while “the sought” is the fly. Another interpretation takes “the seeker” to be the worshipper who seeks benefit through the idol, and “the sought” to be the idol itself. Ibn al-Qayyim (Iʿlām al-Muwaqqiʿīn, 1: 139–140) considers the expression broad enough to encompass all these meanings: weak are the worshipper and the object of worship, the one from whom something is snatched and the one who snatches it. As such, the image gathers every party involved in this false worship under the description of weakness, making the folly of associating such helpless beings with the All-Powerful, All-Prevailing unmistakable (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Shawkānī, al-Saʿdī).
They did not esteem Allah as much as He should rightly be esteemed; verily, Allah surely is All-Powerful, All-Prevailing.[1]

[1] “All-Powerful, All-Prevailing” brings the contrast in the parable to its culmination. God is perfectly Powerful, Able to create whatever He Wills, unconquerable in His Dominion, and prevailing over all things; nothing can wrest anything from His Possession. How different are the false gods of the Associators, which can neither create even a fly nor prevent it from snatching something from them. As a result, the juxtaposition exposes the absurdity of invoking such powerless beings besides the One Who possesses absolute Power and irresistible Dominion (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn Kathīr).
[1]Allah selects[2] Messengers from among the angels and from among people;[3] indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.[4]

[1] This aya answers several of the Associators’ preceding errors at once. They had looked to their idols for support, although those idols are utterly powerless, and they had rejected the Messenger (ﷺ), partly because they found it inconceivable that a human being should be chosen as a Messenger and demanded instead that angels be sent. God now declares that He Alone selects Messengers, from among both angels and humans, according to His Will and Wisdom. Angels are therefore His chosen Messengers, not partners in Divinity, while human Messengers are likewise selected by Him to convey His Message. The explicit placement of “Allah” at the beginning of “Allah selects” further conveys exclusivity: it is God Alone Who determines whom to select; this choice does not belong to people, nor may they dictate to Him whom His Messengers should be (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] “Selects” renders yaṣṭafī. The verb denotes choosing and setting apart what is especially pure or choice. Iṣṭifāʾ is the selection of the finest or purest from among others, and its root, ṣ-f-w, conveys purity and freedom from admixture. The expression thus carries a more discriminating sense than mere choosing: God selects those whom He knows to be especially suited to bear His Message (cf. Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt).
 [3] God selects Messengers from among the angels, including those whom He sends to His Prophets and to whomever He Wills among His servants, and He likewise selects Messengers from among people to impart His Revelation to humanity (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī).
 [4] “All-Hearing, All-Seeing” explains the perfection and exclusivity of God’s selection. He hears all things and sees all things, including the words, conditions, qualities, and hidden realities of His servants, and therefore Knows precisely who among His creation is suited to be selected for His Message. Ergo, His selection of Messengers proceeds from perfect and all-encompassing Knowledge of their fitness to bear and convey that Message. However discerning human beings may be, they cannot penetrate all hidden realities or fully perceive the qualities and shortcomings of those they might choose for the highest offices. How much more absurd, then, is the selection of lifeless stones as objects of worship. Hence, God Alone possesses the right of selection, for His Knowledge Alone encompasses all things (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
[1]He Knows what lies before them and what lies behind them;[2] and to Allah all matters are returned.[3]

[1] This confirms the preceding declaration that God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing, for nothing whatsoever is hidden from His Knowledge. The statement also implicitly calls people to remain mindful of their Lord in secret and in public, since no hidden matter, inward condition, or outward deed escapes Him (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [2] The pronoun has been understood as referring specifically to the selected angelic and human Messengers. Ibn ʿĀshīūr gives two alternatives: the Associators mentioned earlier, or the angels and humans mentioned in the preceding aya. God’s Knowledge encompasses all that concerns them, before them and after them. The expression has also been understood more broadly as encompassing what preceded their creation and what will come after them, their affairs in the Hereafter and in this world, or the deeds they have performed and the deeds and continuing effects they have left behind. All these interpretations affirm the comprehensiveness of God’s Knowledge and reinforce the preceding statement that He is All-Hearing, All-Seeing (cf. Muqātil Ibn Sulaymān, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Shawkānī, al-Qāsimī).
 [3] This emphasises that all affairs ultimately return to God Alone. He sends the Messengers to call people to Him, and people then either respond to their call or reject it, by acting upon the Message or turning away from it. The duty of the Messengers is to convey and call, while judgement and recompense belong to God Alone. On the Day of Judgement, He will judge between His servants and recompense their deeds with perfect Justice, while His gracious Favour may exceed what their deeds merit (cf. al-Ṭabarī, Abīū al-Suʿīūd, al-Saʿdī): “To Allah belongs the Unseen of the Heavens and Earth; all affairs shall be returned to Him. So [Muhammad] worship Him and put your trust in Him, verily your Lord is not unaware of what you [people] do!” (11: 123).
[1]O you who Believe, bow and prostrate,[2] worship your Lord, and do good, [3] so that you may succeed۩[4].

[1] These closing ayas may be read on two complementary levels. In their general and enduring sense, after the preceding address has confronted the Deniers and Associators with the futility of false worship and called them to recognise the Truth, the address now turns to the Believers and calls them to act upon that recognition. They are commanded to bow and prostrate, worship their Lord, do good, strive for Allah, establish the Prayer, give zakat, and hold fast to Him. The sura thus moves in its conclusion from exposing false worship to setting forth the demands of true servanthood. Read within the architecture of the sura, the commands acquire particular force in the circumstances of the first Believers. Earlier, the Believers had been granted permission to fight because they had been wronged and expelled from their homes (22: 39–40), while the sura had already condemned those who barred people from the Sacred Mosque (22: 25). The promise associated with their eventual empowerment is that they will “keep up the Prayer, give zakat [willingly], enjoin virtue, and advise against what is unacceptable” (22: 41). The conclusion now returns strikingly to the same constellation of ideas: striving for God, Prayer, zakat, and reliance upon Him. Against this background, “strive in the cause of Allah with the striving due to Him” may be heard, for the first Believers, as a summons to undertake the struggle through which the Sacred House would ultimately be restored to the worship and rites for which it had been established. Overall, the sura has travelled from exclusion from the Sacred House and permission to resist oppression to the moral and spiritual qualifications of those who will bear responsibility for God’s religion. The ensuing reference to “the creed of your father Ibrāhīm (Abraham)” acquires particular resonance in this same architecture. Ibn ʿĀshīūr says that the reference both exalts this religion and urges adherence to it by emphasising its continuity with the religion of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) (عليه السلام). This recalls the earlier Hajj section, where Ibrāhīm (Abraham) (عليه السلام) is commanded to prepare the Sacred House for those who circumambulate it and to proclaim the Hajj (22: 26–27). In the immediate historical context, the description “your father Ibrāhīm” carries a pointed implication: the Believers who follow his creed of pure submission stand in genuine continuity with his religious inheritance, whereas the Associators, despite their physical custody of the Sacred House, have departed from the very monotheism for which it was founded. The statement “He named you Muslims before and in this [Qur’an]” reinforces this continuity of submission; the preferred referent of “He” is God, not Ibrāhīm, as Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī and other exegetes explicitly argue. All in all, the ending gathers the sura’s major strands into a single response required from the Believers. The Deniers have been called to see the Truth; the Believers are now called to embody it. Their response extends from the inward ikhbāt of the heart to the bodily humility of bowing and prostration, from worship to every form of good, from receiving the religion to striving to uphold it, and from Abrahamic belonging to the responsibility of bearing witness before humanity. Their selection is consequently a commission as much as an honour. Appropriately, the sura does not end with human strength, but with Prayer, zakat, holding fast to God, and complete dependence upon Him: “He is your Protector; excellent is the Protector and excellent is the Granter of victory.” Ibn ʿĀshīūr regards these final words as a particularly apt and beautiful conclusion to the sura (Ibn ʿĀshīūr, cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī, al-Saʿdī).
 [2] “Bow and prostrate” refers particularly to bowing and prostrating in Prayer, while also expressing the profound humility and submission embodied in these acts. The Believers are thus commanded to humble themselves before their Lord in obedience and to worship Him with complete sincerity and devotion (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [3] “Do good” encompasses every kind of good that God has commanded the Believers to perform. “So that you may succeed” points to attaining what they hope for in this world and the Hereafter and being saved from what they fear. Success therefore comprises both the attainment of what is desirable and deliverance from what is harmful (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Shawkānī, al-Saʿdī).
 [4] “Succeed” signifies tufliḥīūn, from the root f-l-ḥ. Falāḥ carries a richer sense than ordinary success. Ibn Fāris traces one of the root’s fundamental meanings to success and continuance, while Ibn Qutaybah relates falāḥ particularly to abiding and explains the mufliḥīūn as those who attain lasting bliss. al-Iṣfahānī defines falāḥ as attaining one’s sought end and distinguishes between its worldly and Hereafter dimensions. The word thus combines attaining what is desired, escaping what is feared, and enduring in the good thereby attained (cf. Ibn Qutaybah, Gharīb al-QurÒān; Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lughah; al-Sijistānī, Gharīb al-QurÒān; al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt; al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr). The wording also prepares directly for the opening of the following Sura: “The Believers have indeed succeeded” (23: 1). What is presented here as the hoped-for outcome of bowing, prostration, worshipping God, and doing good is announced there as an accomplished reality and then detailed through the defining qualities of the Believers. al-Suyīūṭī expressly draws attention to this correspondence, observing that the general statement at the end of Sura al-Ḥajj is elaborated at the beginning of Sura al-MuÒminīūn (cf. al-Suyīūṭī, Asrār Tartīb al-QurÒān).

And strive in the cause of Allah with the striving due to Him.[1] He has specially set you apart[2] and has placed no hardship upon you in religion.[3] [Adhere to] the creed of your father Ibrāhīm (Abraham).[4] He named you Muslims before and in this [Qur’an],[5] so that the Messenger may be a witness over you and you may be witnesses over people.[6] So keep up the Prayer, give zakat,[7] and hold fast to Allah.[8] He is your Protector; excellent is the Protector and excellent is the Granter of victory.[9]

[1] “Strive in the cause of Allah with the striving due to Him” has been understood both specifically and comprehensively. According to the first interpretation, jihād here refers primarily to fighting in the Path of God, which al-Ṭabarī regards as the predominant usage of the term. Based on the broader interpretation, it encompasses every form of striving in obedience to God: striving against the self and its desires, against Satan and his whisperings, against Deniers and their Denial, and against wrongdoing and deviation, through one’s wealth, person, speech, and action. “With the striving due to Him” further conveys exerting one’s utmost capacity with complete sincerity for God’s sake; it combines earnest endeavour, purity of intention, and fulfilling what is due to Him, each according to one’s ability (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Abīū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr).
 [2] “He has specially set you apart” may be understood as giving the reason for all the preceding commands beginning with “O you who Believe, bow and prostrate”: because God has set them apart for this distinction and responsibility, they are all the more bound to show gratitude by fulfilling what He has commanded. Ijtibāʾ designates a special choosing and setting apart; here, it means that God has set them apart to receive His religion, disseminate it, and support it against those who oppose it. Hence, the address applies primarily to the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ), who first bore this responsibility in the circumstances of Revelation, while extending to subsequent generations of Believers insofar as they share the same defining qualities and obligations. The expression may also carry the sense that this community has been specially favoured over earlier communities (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr). This special setting apart of the Believing community is elsewhere connected with the responsibility of serving God and conveying His religion: “You are indeed the best nation the world has seen: you enjoin virtue, advise against what is unacceptable and Believe in Allah” (3: 110). Abīū ʿInabah al-Khawlānī (رضي الله عنه) narrated that The Prophet (ﷺ) said: “Allah continues to plant in this religion people whom He employs in His obedience” (Ibn Mājah: 8; Aḥmad: 17787). The distinction expressed by “He has specially set you apart” is therefore not merely an honour, but a calling to obedience, service, and the upholding of the religion.
 [3] “He has placed no hardship upon you in religion” further manifests God’s favour towards this community. The religion with which they have been entrusted is one whose obligations are made practicable and free from undue constraint, so that its purposes may be fulfilled without imposing intolerable difficulty upon those who observe it. Ḥaraj literally denotes narrowness or constriction and is here used for hardship and difficulty. This principle of ease recurs elsewhere in the Qur’an: “Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you” (2: 185) and is reflected in the description of Islam as the upright and accommodating religion (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [4] “The creed of your father Ibrāhīm (Abraham)” admits several closely related interpretations. It may be connected with the preceding statement that God has placed no hardship upon the Believers in religion, meaning that He has made their religion broad and accommodating, as was the creed of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) (عليه السلام). It may also carry an implicit command: “[Adhere to] the creed of your father Ibrāhīm”, an interpretation adopted by a number of exegetes and reflected in the translation. al-Shinqīṭī observes that the expression may encompass all the preceding commands, including bowing, prostration, worship, doing good, and striving for God, since all belong to the upright religion of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) (عليه السلام). “Your father” may address the Arabs specifically through their physical descent from Ibrāhīm (Abraham) (عليه السلام), or all Muslims more generally, in view of the reverence and religious affiliation due to him as the father of their monotheistic tradition (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, al-Ṭabarī, al-Samʿānī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Shawkānī, al-Saʿdī, al-Shinqīṭī).
 [5] “He named you Muslims before and in this [Qur’an]” means that God named this community Muslims before the revelation of the Qur’an, in the earlier revealed Books, and likewise named them Muslims in this Qur’an. This is the interpretation attributed to the majority of exegetes. The pronoun “He” therefore refers to God, not to Ibrāhīm (Abraham) (عليه السلام). al-Ṭabarī rejects the latter interpretation on the grounds that Ibrāhīm (Abraham) (عليه السلام) could not have named the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) Muslims “in this [Qur’an]”, which was revealed long after him. al-Shinqīṭī further observes that the sequence of verbs supports the same referent throughout: “He has specially set you apart”, “has placed no hardship upon you in religion”, and “He named you Muslims” all refer to God. As such, the statement places the Muslim community within a continuity of submission extending through the earlier Revelations and culminating in the Qur’an (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn al-Qayyim, Ibn Kathīr, Abīū al-Suʿīūd, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr, al-Shinqīṭī). “He has specially set you apart” is further reflected in the distinctive name He has given them: Muslims. God has honoured this community by singling them out with this noble designation, a name expressing their defining relationship of submission to Him, without denying that earlier Prophets and Believers were also described as Muslims. As a result, their ijtibāʾ is manifested not only in their responsibility to receive and uphold the religion, but also in the very name by which God identifies them (cf. Ibn ʿĀshīūr). In parallel narrations from al-Ḥārith al-Ashʿarī (رضي الله عنه), the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) warned against the partisan calls of the Age of Ignorance, saying in meaning: “Call the Muslims by their names, by what Allah (سبحانه وتعالى) has named them: Muslims, Believers (muÒminīūn), servants of Allah (ʿibād Allāh) (سبحانه وتعالى)” (al-Tirmidhī: 2863; Aḥmad: 17170; al-Nasāʾī, al-Sunan al-Kubrā: 11349). The Ḥadīth thus reinforces the honour and significance of the name mentioned in the aya: it is a Divinely given identity grounded in submission to God, not in tribal, factional, or pre-Islamic affiliation.
 [6] “So that the Messenger may be a witness over you and you may be witnesses over people” explains one purpose of God’s setting this community apart and honouring it with the name “Muslims”. The Messenger (ﷺ) will testify on the Day of Judgement that he conveyed his Lord’s Message to this community, while they will testify concerning the other nations that their Messengers conveyed the Messages God entrusted to them. Another interpretation takes the Messenger’s testimony to concern this community’s faith in him, while al-Shinqīṭī also mentions that he will testify to the truthfulness of their testimony concerning the earlier Messengers. In this regard, the aya presents this community’s distinction as a responsibility of testimony as well as an honour (cf. Muqātil Ibn Sulaymān, al-Ṭabarī, al-Samarqandī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Maḥallī, al-Shawkānī, al-Qāsimī, al-Shinqīṭī). Abīū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (رضي الله عنه) narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, in an abridged narration: “Nīūḥ (Noah) will be called on the Day of Judgement and asked, ‘Did you convey [the Message]?’ He will say, ‘Yes.’ His people will then be asked, ‘Did he convey [the Message] to you?’ They will say, ‘No warner came to us.’ He will be asked, ‘Who will testify for you?’ He will say, ‘Muhammad and his community.’ You will then testify that he conveyed [the Message]”, whereupon The Prophet (ﷺ) recited: “and the Messenger may be a witness over you” (2: 143) (al-Bukhārī: 4487). This Ḥadīth makes explicit that the Muslim community’s witnessing over other nations concerns their testimony that the earlier Messengers faithfully communicated the Messages entrusted to them. Their status as witnesses is clearly another dimension of the responsibility attached to their being specially set apart by God.
 [7] “So keep up the Prayer, give zakat” follows from the great favour just mentioned: God has specially set this community apart, removed hardship from its religion, honoured it with the name “Muslims”, and entrusted it with bearing witness over humanity. Accordingly, the Believers are called to respond to these blessings with gratitude by faithfully maintaining the Prayer with its prescribed conditions and pillars, and by giving the obligatory zakat to those entitled to receive it. The command thereby turns Divine favour into practical responsibility and worship (cf. Muqātil Ibn Sulaymān, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
 [8] “Hold fast to Allah” directly calls for seeking protection and support in God through reliance upon Him. The broader concept of iʿtiṣām also encompasses steadfast adherence to His Revelation. The Believers are commanded to place their trust in Him, seek His help in all their affairs, and hold firmly to what He has revealed. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes these two dimensions of iʿtiṣām: holding fast to God through reliance, seeking aid, entrusting one’s affairs to Him, and taking refuge in Him; and holding fast to His Revelation by submitting to it and governing one’s Belief and conduct by it. The reason follows immediately: “He is your Protector”, the One Who guards them, directs their affairs, and grants them victory over their enemies (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Samarqandī, Ibn al-Qayyim, Madārij al-Sālikīn; Ibn Kathīr, al-Shawkānī, al-Saʿdī).
 [9] “Excellent is the Granter of victory”, alternatively, “Excellent is the Helper”, constitutes niʿma al-naṣīr. Naṣīr is more intensive than the ordinary active participle nāṣir, expressing abundant and powerful support. Here, its attribution to God affirms that His help is perfect and unfailing. The expression also brings to completion a recurring theme of the sura. When the Believers were first permitted to fight after being wronged and driven from their homes, they were assured that “Allah is indeed fully Able to grant them victory” (22: 39), followed by the promise: “Allah will surely grant victory to whoever supports Him” (22: 40). Conversely, the wrongdoers are told that they will have “no helper” (22: 71). The sura now closes by commanding the Believers to strive for God and to hold fast to Him, then declaring Him the excellent Naṣīr. Their striving is therefore the duty entrusted to them, while victory ultimately comes from God Alone. In the historical movement of the Sura, this also resonates with the struggle of the first Believers, who had been expelled from their homes and barred from the Sacred Mosque, and with the promised restoration of their ability to establish worship and the Abrahamic rites (cf. al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Saʿdī, Ibn ʿĀshīūr).
